question: From a group of 7 women and 6 men, 5 persons are required to form a selection committee in which at least 3 women should be there. How many are the possibilities?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Combinatorics / Committee Selection with Constraints:
  • Given: 7 women and 6 men. A selection committee of 5 persons is to be formed containing at least 3 women.
  • Cases:
    • Case 1 (3 Women and 2 Men): $$\binom{7}{3} \times \binom{6}{2} = \frac{7 \times 6 \times 5}{3 \times 2 \times 1} \times \frac{6 \times 5}{2 \times 1} = 35 \times 15 = 525$$
    • Case 2 (4 Women and 1 Man): $$\binom{7}{4} \times \binom{6}{1} = \binom{7}{3} \times 6 = 35 \times 6 = 210$$
    • Case 3 (5 Women and 0 Men): $$\binom{7}{5} \times \binom{6}{0} = \binom{7}{2} \times 1 = \frac{7 \times 6}{2 \times 1} = 21$$
  • Total Possibilities: $$\text{Total} = 525 + 210 + 21 = \mathbf{756}$$

question: Two trains, one from Delhi to Pune and the other from Pune to Delhi, start at the same time from their respective stations. After they meet, the trains reach their appropriate destinations after 4 hours and 9 hours respectively. The ratio of their speeds is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Relative Motion and Speed Ratio of Trains:
  • Formula for Trains Meeting and Continuing to Destinations: If two objects start at the same time from two points $A$ and $B$ towards each other, and after meeting they take time $t_1$ and $t_2$ respectively to reach their opposite destinations, the ratio of their speeds is given by: $$\mathbf{\frac{S_1}{S_2} = \sqrt{\frac{t_2}{t_1}}}$$
  • Calculation: Given $t_1 = 4\text{ hours}$ and $t_2 = 9\text{ hours}$: $$\frac{S_1}{S_2} = \sqrt{\frac{9}{4}} = \mathbf{\frac{3}{2} = 3:2}$$

question: A container has a mixture of kerosene and water in a ratio of 7 : 5. When 9 litres of mixture are taken off and the container is filled with 9 litres of water, the ratio between kerosene and water becomes 7 : 9. How many litres of kerosene were initially in the container?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Mixture and Replacement Calculation:
  • Initial Ratio: Kerosene : Water = $7 : 5$. Let initial volume of kerosene $= 7x$ and water $= 5x$. Total mixture $= 12x$.
  • Withdrawal of 9 Litres:
    • Kerosene removed $= 9 \times \frac{7}{12} = \frac{21}{4}\text{ litres}$
    • Water removed $= 9 \times \frac{5}{12} = \frac{15}{4}\text{ litres}$
  • Addition of 9 Litres of Water: $$\frac{7x - \frac{21}{4}}{5x - \frac{15}{4} + 9} = \frac{7}{9}$$ $$\frac{28x - 21}{20x + 21} = \frac{7}{9}$$ $$9(28x - 21) = 7(20x + 21)$$ $$252x - 189 = 140x + 147$$ $$112x = 336 \implies x = 3$$
  • Initial Kerosene: $7x = 7 \times 3 = \mathbf{21\text{ litres}}$.

question: The missing number in the series 40, 120, 60, 180, 90, ___, 135 is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Alternating Number Series:
  • Given series: $40, 120, 60, 180, 90, \underline{\quad}, 135$
  • Pattern: $$40 \times 3 = 120$$ $$120 \div 2 = 60$$ $$60 \times 3 = 180$$ $$180 \div 2 = 90$$ $$\mathbf{90 \times 3 = 270}$$ $$270 \div 2 = 135$$
  • The missing number is 270.

question: Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F are standing in a circle facing the centre of the circle. B is between F and C, A is between E and D, F is to the left of D. Who is between A and F?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Circular Seating Arrangement:
  • Six persons $A, B, C, D, E, F$ face the center of a circle.
  • "B is between F and C" $\implies$ sequence is $F - B - C$ (or $C - B - F$).
  • "F is to the left of D" $\implies$ looking towards center, $D$ is clockwise next to $F$, with $F$ to $D$'s left.
  • "A is between E and D" $\implies$ sequence is $E - A - D$.
  • Tracing the full clockwise circle: $F \to B \to C \to E \to A \to D \to F$.
  • Looking at the position between $A$ and $F$, we see D is seated directly between $A$ and $F$.

question: The molecular weight of a protein is 30 kDa. The minimal length of mRNA encoding this polypeptide will be close to
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Polypeptide Molecular Weight to mRNA Length Calculation:
  • Average Molecular Weight of an Amino Acid: Approximately $110\text{ Da}$ (accounting for the loss of a water molecule during peptide bond formation).
  • Number of Amino Acids: $$n_{\text{aa}} = \frac{30,000\text{ Da}}{110\text{ Da/aa}} \approx 272.7 \approx 273\text{ amino acids}$$
  • Nucleotides Required: Each amino acid is encoded by a triplet codon of 3 nucleotides: $$\text{Coding nucleotides} = 273 \times 3 = 819\text{ nucleotides}$$ Adding stop codon ($+3$) yields $\sim 822\text{ nucleotides}$.
  • Among the given options, the closest minimal length is 800.

question: What is the amount of protein required to prepare 5 ml of 1μM solution (Mol. Wt. of protein is 25 kDa)?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Molar Solution Preparation:
  • Given:
    • Volume ($V$) = $5\text{ mL} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ L}$
    • Concentration ($C$) = $1\ \mu\text{M} = 10^{-6}\text{ mol/L}$
    • Molecular Weight ($MW$) = $25\text{ kDa} = 25,000\text{ g/mol}$
  • Moles of Protein Required ($n$): $$n = C \times V = 10^{-6}\text{ mol/L} \times 5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ L} = 5 \times 10^{-9}\text{ moles}$$
  • Mass Required ($m$): $$m = n \times MW = 5 \times 10^{-9}\text{ mol} \times 25,000\text{ g/mol} = 1.25 \times 10^{-4}\text{ g}$$ $$m = 1.25 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^6\ \mu\text{g} = \mathbf{125\ \mu\text{g}}$$

question: Calculate the concentration of NADH solution, whose A340nm = 0.8 O.D. (optical path length is 10 mm, NADH molar extinction coefficient is Ɛ340 = 6220)
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Beer-Lambert Law Spectrophotometric Concentration Calculation:
  • Beer-Lambert Law: $$A = \varepsilon \cdot c \cdot l \implies c = \frac{A}{\varepsilon \cdot l}$$
  • Given:
    • Absorbance at $340\text{ nm}$ ($A$) = $0.8$
    • Optical path length ($l$) = $10\text{ mm} = 1\text{ cm}$
    • Molar extinction coefficient ($\varepsilon_{340}$) = $6220\text{ M}^{-1}\cdot\text{cm}^{-1}$
  • Calculation: $$c = \frac{0.8}{6220 \times 1} = 1.286 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M} = \mathbf{128.6\ \mu\text{M}}$$

question: If counting was done in base 5 (instead of 10) so that 5 (in base 10) would be written as 10 (in base 5), 6 (in base 10) would be written as 11 (in base 5), then 89 (in base 10) will be written as which of the following numbers in base 5?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Base Conversion (Base 10 to Base 5):
  • To convert 89 from decimal (base 10) to base 5, perform successive divisions by 5 and record the remainders: $$89 \div 5 = 17 \quad \text{with remainder } \mathbf{4}$$ $$17 \div 5 = 3 \quad \text{with remainder } \mathbf{2}$$ $$3 \div 5 = 0 \quad \text{with remainder } \mathbf{3}$$
  • Reading remainders from bottom to top: $\mathbf{324_5}$.

question: If there are 3 children in a family, then the probability that there is only one girl child in the family is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Binomial Probability of Child Sex:
  • In a family with 3 children, each child is independently a boy ($B$) or a girl ($G$) with $p = 1/2$.
  • Total outcomes $= 2^3 = 8$: $$\{BBB, BBG, BGB, GBB, BGG, GBG, GGB, GGG\}$$
  • Favorable outcomes with exactly one girl: $$\{BBG, BGB, GBB\} \implies 3\text{ outcomes}$$
  • Probability = $\mathbf{\frac{3}{8}}$.

question: A students average marks (arithmetic mean) on three tests is 80. Which of the following CANNOT be the number of tests on which (s)he earned exactly 80 marks?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Arithmetic Mean and Test Score Distribution:
  • Average on three tests is 80: $$\text{Total Marks} = 80 \times 3 = 240$$
  • If the student scored exactly 80 on two tests: $$80 + 80 + T_3 = 240 \implies T_3 = 240 - 160 = 80$$
  • If two tests are 80, the third test must also be 80! Therefore, the student either earned 80 on 0 tests, 1 test, or all 3 tests. It is mathematically impossible to have earned 80 on exactly 2 tests.

question: If 0<a<b<1,which of the following is INCORRECT? Option 1 Option 2 Option 3 Option 4
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Inequalities for Numbers Between 0 and 1:
  • Given: $0 < a < b < 1$. Both $a$ and $b$ are positive fractions, and $a < b$.
  • Evaluating Option 3: Since $a < b$, taking the reciprocals reverses the inequality: $$\frac{1}{a} > \frac{1}{b} \implies \frac{1}{b} - \frac{1}{a} < 0$$
  • Therefore, the statement $\mathbf{\frac{1}{b} - \frac{1}{a} > 0}$ is INCORRECT.

question: If 25% of 260 equals 6.5% of 10 a , what is a?
explanation:

  • Given: $25\% \text{ of } 260 = 6.5\% \text{ of } 10^a$

  • $$65 = 0.065 \times 10^a$$
  • $$10^a = \frac{65}{0.065} = 1000 = 10^3 \implies \mathbf{a = 3}$$

question: In an experiment evaluating DNA replication by CsCl density gradient centrifugation after one generation of growth in 14N medium, the observation of two distinct bands corresponding to purely heavy (15N) parental DNA and purely light (14N) newly synthesized DNA supports which model of replication?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Meselson-Stahl Experiment and Models of DNA Replication:
  • In 1958, Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli in heavy isotope $^{15}\text{N}$ and transferred them to light $^{14}\text{N}$ medium.
  • Predictions after One Generation:
    • Semi-conservative: Yields a single intermediate hybrid band ($^{14}\text{N}\text{-}^{15}\text{N}$).
    • Conservative: Yields two distinct bands—one heavy parental band ($^{15}\text{N}\text{-}^{15}\text{N}$) and one light newly synthesized band ($^{14}\text{N}\text{-}^{14}\text{N}$).
    • Dispersive: Yields a single hybrid band.
  • Therefore, observing two distinct bands (one purely heavy and one purely light) after one generation supports the conservative replication model.

question: What will come in place of (*) in the following number series? 19, 26, 40, 68, 124 (*)
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Differences in Number Series:
  • Series: $19, 26, 40, 68, 124, (*)$
  • Differences between consecutive terms: $$26 - 19 = 7$$ $$40 - 26 = 14 = 7 \times 2$$ $$68 - 40 = 28 = 14 \times 2$$ $$124 - 68 = 56 = 28 \times 2$$
  • The next difference must be $56 \times 2 = 112$.
  • Next term = $124 + 112 = \mathbf{236}$.

question: Fifty-three percent of a number is 358 less than the square of 26.What is the value of three-fourth of 23 per cent of that number?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Algebraic Percentage Calculation:
  • Square of 26 = $26^2 = 676$.
  • $53\%$ of a number $x$ is 358 less than 676: $$0.53x = 676 - 358 = 318 \implies x = \frac{318}{0.53} = 600$$
  • The problem asks for $17.25\%$ of this number: $$\text{Value} = 600 \times 0.1725 = \mathbf{103.5}$$

question: A cube is painted on all sides using yellow and black color such that opposite faces are painted in different color. This cube is cut into 27 smaller cubes of equal sizes. How many smaller cubes will have only one face colored?

question: A man fills a basket with eggs in such a way that the number of eggs added on each successive day is the same as the number already present in the basket. This way the basket gets completely filled in 24 days. After how many days the basket was 1 / 4th full?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Exponential Doubling Time Problem:
  • The number of eggs in the basket doubles every minute.
  • The basket becomes completely full ($100\%$ capacity) in 24 minutes.
  • Working backward:
    • At 23 minutes (1 minute before), the basket was half full ($1/2 = 50\%$).
    • At 22 minutes (2 minutes before), the basket was one-fourth full ($1/4 = 25\%$).
  • Therefore, the basket was $1/4$ full at 22 minutes.

question: Seema goes 30 km towards North from a fixed point, then after turning to her right she goes 15 km. After this she turns right again and goes another 30 km. How far and in what direction is she from her starting point?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Direction and Displacement Vector Problem:
  • Seema travels $30\text{ km}$ North ($+30\hat{j}$).
  • Turns right (East) and travels $15\text{ km}$ ($+15\hat{i}$).
  • Turns right (South) and travels $30\text{ km}$ ($-30\hat{j}$).
  • Net displacement $= 30\hat{j} + 15\hat{i} - 30\hat{j} = +15\hat{i}$.
  • She is 15 km East of her starting point.

question: Th1 response is characterized by the secretion of which of the following combinations of cytokines?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Cytokine Profile of Th1 Immune Responses:
  • Th1 Cells: CD4+ T helper 1 cells drive cell-mediated immunity to eliminate intracellular pathogens (such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Leishmania).
  • Cytokines:
    • IL-12: Secreted by dendritic cells and macrophages, acts on naive T cells to induce Th1 differentiation via STAT4 and T-bet.
    • IFN-$\gamma$: The signature effector cytokine secreted by Th1 cells, which potently activates macrophages (classical M1 activation) to upregulate iNOS, ROS, and phagolysosomal killing.
  • Therefore, Th1 responses are characterized by IFN-$\gamma$ and IL-12.

question: In hybridoma production, aminopterin is added after fusion to
options: ensure monoclonality of the cultures that survive .
cause the death of non -antibody secreting hybrids.
cause the death of unfused myeloma cells.
cause the death of unfused splenic cells.
correct_answer: cause the death of unfused myeloma cells.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] HAT Selection in Monoclonal Antibody Hybridoma Production:
  • Hybridoma Technology (Kohler & Milstein): Splenic B cells are fused with HGPRT-deficient myeloma cells using polyethylene glycol (PEG).
  • Role of Aminopterin: Aminopterin is a folate analog that irreversibly blocks dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), shutting down the de novo purine and pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis pathway.
  • Cells are forced to rely on the salvage pathway using Hypoxanthine and Thymidine, which requires the enzyme HGPRT.
  • Unfused myeloma cells lack HGPRT ($HGPRT^-$) and cannot synthesize DNA, causing them to die within days. Only hybridomas (which inherited HGPRT from the B cell and immortality from the myeloma) survive on HAT medium.

question: An alpha-helical conformation of a globular protein can be determined by
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Circular Dichroism (CD) Determination of Secondary Structure:
  • Far-UV Circular Dichroism (190–250 nm): Measures the differential absorption of left- and right-circularly polarized light by chiral peptide bond amide chromophores.
  • $\alpha$-Helical Signature: An $\alpha$-helix displays a unique CD spectrum characterized by two pronounced negative minima at 208 nm and 222 nm, and a strong positive peak at $\sim 193\text{ nm}$.
  • This makes CD spectroscopy the most rapid and definitive biophysical method for determining the $\alpha$-helical content of proteins in solution.

question: The athymic nude (nu/nu) mice are difficult to breed and maintain because the homozygous (nu/nu) females are sterile. How will you propagate it to get maximum nude (nu/nu) mice progeny.
options: by mating of normal males to heterozygous (nu/+) females.
by mating homozygous (nu/nu) males to heterozygous (nu/+) females.
by mating of heterozygous (nu/+) males to heterozygous (nu/+) females.
by mating of heterozygous (nu/+) males to normal females.
correct_answer: by mating homozygous (nu/nu) males to heterozygous (nu/+) females.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Breeding Colony Maintenance of Athymic Nude Mice:
  • Nude Mice ($Foxn1^{nu}$): Homozygous mutant mice ($nu/nu$) lack a functional thymus (athymic, severely T-cell deficient) and are hairless.
  • Maternal Infertility: Homozygous nude females ($nu/nu$) have defective mammary gland development, poor lactation, and fail to nurse litters adequately.
  • To maintain viable breeding colonies, fertile homozygous males ($nu/nu$) are mated to fertile heterozygous females ($nu/+$), yielding $50\%$ nude ($nu/nu$) and $50\%$ haired carrier ($nu/+$) offspring.

question: The base sequence of a short piece of DNA is AGCTTACG. During replication, a transition mutation occurs in the complementary strand synthesized on this piece of DNA. Which of the following is mutated complementary strand?
options: T C G A A T C G
T C G A A T G C
C G C G A G C T
U C G A A G U C
correct_answer: C G C G A G C T
explanation:
[CONCEPT] DNA Complementarity and Base Pairing:
  • Watson-Crick base pairing dictates that Adenine pairs with Thymine ($A-T$) and Guanine pairs with Cytosine ($G-C$).
  • Given template $5'\text{-AGCTTACG-}3'$, the complementary daughter strand is $3'\text{-TCGAATGC-}5'$, which corresponds to $5'\text{-CGTAAGCT-}3'$ or the matching nucleotide option.

question: Uncoupling of LDL receptors with their ligands occur at which of the following compartments?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] LDL Receptor Uncoupling in Receptor-Mediated Endocytosis:
  • LDL particles bind cell-surface LDL receptors and are internalized via clathrin-coated vesicles.
  • The vesicles fuse to form the early endosome (sorting endosome), where vacuolar $H^+$-ATPases pump protons to lower the internal pH to $\sim 6.0\text{--}6.5$.
  • This mildly acidic pH protonates histidine residues in the $\beta$-propeller domain of the LDL receptor, causing a conformational change that releases the bound LDL particle into the lumen while the receptor recycles back to the plasma membrane.

question: Transport of cargo from nucleus to cytoplasm through nuclear pore is regulated by
explanation:

  • Directional transport of macromolecules across the Nuclear Pore Complex (NPC) is governed by the Ran GTPase cycle.
  • Export Mechanism: Inside the nucleus, RanGEF (RCC1) maintains Ran in the GTP-bound state (RanGTP). RanGTP binds exportin and cargo to form a stable ternary export complex. After traversing the NPC into the cytoplasm, RanGAP stimulates GTP hydrolysis to RanGDP, triggering complex disassembly and cargo release.

question: Which one of the following is a cobalt containing vitamin?
explanation:

  • Vitamin $B_{12}$ (Cobalamin): The only vitamin that contains a metal trace element.
  • Its chemical structure features a corrin ring coordinating a central cobalt ($Co$) ion, which forms an organometallic bond with a methyl or $5'$-deoxyadenosyl group to act as an essential cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

question: Brefeldin A inhibits protein transport from
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Brefeldin A Mechanism of Action:
  • Brefeldin A (BFA): A fungal macrocyclic lactone antibiotic that specifically inhibits the guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for Arf1 (ADP-ribosylation factor 1).
  • Inactivation of Arf1 prevents the assembly of COP-I coatomer protein complexes onto Golgi membranes, causing the rapid collapse and resorption of the Golgi apparatus into the endoplasmic reticulum, effectively blocking protein vesicular trafficking from the ER to the Golgi apparatus.

question: Which one of the following diseases is caused by a bacteria ?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Bacterial Etiology of Tetanus:
  • Tetanus (Lockjaw): A severe infectious disease caused by the obligate anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive bacterium Clostridium tetani.
  • The bacterium produces tetanospasmin, a potent neurotoxin that cleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP) in inhibitory interneurons (Renshaw cells), blocking the release of GABA and glycine, causing spastic muscle paralysis.

question: Which one of the following antibiotics is used to demonstrate the new/fresh protein synthesis in response to an inducer/ upon induction in a microbial system?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chloramphenicol as a Protein Synthesis Inhibitor:
  • Chloramphenicol: A broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotic that binds reversibly to the 50S ribosomal subunit of prokaryotes, blocking the peptidyl transferase reaction and terminating peptide chain elongation.
  • In molecular biology experiments, chloramphenicol is used to demonstrate whether biological responses (such as viral replication or enzyme induction) require de novo protein synthesis.

question: Both somatic hypermutation and isotype switching depend upon a highly specific enzyme of adaptive immunity that is made only by B cells proliferating in response to antigen. The name of the enzyme is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Activation-Induced Cytidine Deaminase (AID) in Antibody Maturation:
  • Both Somatic Hypermutation (SHM) and Class Switch Recombination (CSR) in antigen-activated B cells depend on the master DNA mutator enzyme Activation-Induced Cytidine Deaminase (AID).
  • AID deaminates deoxycytidine ($dC$) to deoxyuracil ($dU$) in single-stranded DNA during transcription of immunoglobulin variable and switch regions, creating $U:G$ mismatches that initiate error-prone repair and double-strand breaks for isotype switching.

question: AGO proteins are associated with
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Argonaute (AGO) Proteins in the RNAi Effector Complex:
  • Argonaute family proteins (AGO) are the central catalytic core components of the RNA-Induced Silencing Complex (RISC).
  • The PAZ domain of AGO binds the $3'$-end of small regulatory RNAs (siRNA or miRNA), while its RNase H-like PIWI domain provides the endonucleolytic "slicer" activity that cleaves target mRNA transcripts with complementary sequences.

question: The fusion between protoplasts can be enhanced by subjecting them to
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Electrofusion of Plant Protoplasts:
  • Protoplast Fusion: In somatic hybridization, isolated plant protoplasts are fused by subjecting them to electrofusion.
  • A low-amplitude, high-frequency AC field first aligns protoplasts in dielectrophoretic chains ("pearl-chain formation"). A subsequent short, high-voltage DC electric pulse transiently breaks down the membrane bilayers (electroporation), promoting cytoplasmic continuity and somatic hybrid fusion.

question: If a nucleotide sequence encoding a protein is known and a homologous protein to be identified, which of the following will be the best analysis tool?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] BLASTn for Nucleotide Sequence Similarity:
  • When a nucleotide sequence is known and a researcher seeks to find homologous nucleotide sequences in GenBank, the appropriate tool is BLASTn (nucleotide query against nucleotide database).
  • BLASTp compares protein to protein; BLASTx translates a nucleotide query in 6 frames to search a protein database; tBLASTn compares a protein query against a translated nucleotide database.

question: The concentration of which of the following plays an important role in somatic embryogenesis?
explanation:

question: Simple sequence repeats (SSRs) markers are derived from
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genomic Distribution of SSR (Microsatellite) Markers:
  • Simple Sequence Repeats (SSRs): Tandem repeats of 1 to 6 nucleotide motifs (e.g., $(CA)_n$, $(GATA)_n$).
  • Although most abundant in non-coding regions (introns, intergenic spacers, and UTRs), SSRs also occur within coding exonic sequences (typically triplet repeats like $(CAG)_n$ to prevent frameshifts). Thus, SSR markers are derived from both coding and non-coding sequences.

question: Which of the following enzymes are required for making plant protoplasts?
explanation:

  • Plant cell walls consist of cellulose microfibrils embedded in a cross-linked matrix of hemicellulose and pectin (middle lamella).
  • To isolate viable protoplasts, plant tissues are incubated with a combination of cellulase (to digest cellulose microfibrils) and pectinase (to dissolve the pectinaceous middle lamella cementing adjacent cells together).

question: The floral dip method is commonly used for

The bacterium transforms the female gametophyte inside the ovules, producing transgenic seeds without needing in vitro tissue culture regeneration.

question: Impeller Reynolds number is given by
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Impeller Reynolds Number ($Re_i$):
  • In stirred tank reactors, the impeller Reynolds number characterizes fluid flow around the agitator: $$\mathbf{Re_i = \frac{\rho \cdot N \cdot D_i^2}{\mu} = \frac{D^2 N \rho}{\mu}}$$ where $D_i$ is impeller diameter, $N$ is rotational speed, $\rho$ is broth density, and $\mu$ is broth viscosity.

question: Continuous cultivation is carried out in 10 L working volume. If 0.2 h-1 dilution rate has to be maintained, then the feed rate will be
explanation:

  • Dilution Rate ($D$): $$D = \frac{F}{V} \implies F = D \times V$$
  • Given: Working volume $V = 10\text{ L}$ and dilution rate $D = 0.2\text{ h}^{-1}$.
  • Feed Flow Rate ($F$): $$F = 0.2\text{ h}^{-1} \times 10\text{ L} = \mathbf{2\text{ L/h}}$$

question: If the doubling time of an organism is 0.693 h, the specific growth rate will be
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Specific Growth Rate from Doubling Time:
  • The relationship between doubling time ($t_d$) and specific growth rate ($\mu$) in exponential growth is: $$t_d = \frac{\ln 2}{\mu} = \frac{0.693}{\mu} \implies \mu = \frac{0.693}{t_d}$$
  • Given $t_d = 0.693\text{ h}$: $$\mu = \frac{0.693}{0.693\text{ h}} = \mathbf{1\text{ h}^{-1}}$$

question: Aeration in a fermentor is expressed as VVM. What will be the VVM if air is sparged at 2000 L/min with a working volume 10 m3?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] VVM (Volume of Air per Volume of Liquid per Minute):
  • Definition: $$\text{VVM} = \frac{\text{Volumetric Air Flow Rate (L/min)}}{\text{Liquid Volume in Fermentor (L)}}$$
  • Given air flow = $2\text{ L/min}$ and reactor liquid volume = $10\text{ L}$: $$\text{VVM} = \frac{2\text{ L/min}}{10\text{ L}} = \mathbf{0.2}$$

question: Rate of centrifugation of a particle in a centrifuge is increased by
options: Decreasing the density difference between the particle and liquid
Increasing the viscosity of suspended fluid
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Sedimentation Rate in Centrifugation:
  • The terminal sedimentation velocity ($v$) of a spherical particle in a centrifugal field is given by Svedberg's equation: $$v = \frac{d^2 (\rho_p - \rho_m) \omega^2 r}{18\mu}$$
  • Because velocity is directly proportional to the square of angular velocity ($\omega^2$), the most effective way to increase the rate of particle sedimentation is by increasing the centrifuge speed.

question: In a batch process of solvent-solvent extraction, higher percentage of extraction is ensured when the whole solvent for extraction is added
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Efficiency of Multi-Stage Liquid-Liquid Extraction:
  • In batch solvent extraction, extracting multiple times with smaller portions of solvent (e.g., four times in equal volume) achieves a substantially higher cumulative recovery of solute than performing a single extraction using the entire volume of solvent, due to the partition coefficient equilibrium ($K = C_1 / C_2$).

question: Which one of the following is true during the separation of biomolecules by reversed phase chromatography ?
options: Stationary phase is less polar than the mobile phase
Stationary phase is more polar than the mobile phase
Both the stationary and the mobile phase are having the same polarity
Polarity of the mobile phase does not play any role
correct_answer: Stationary phase is less polar than the mobile phase
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Reversed-Phase Chromatography (RPC) Principle:
  • In reversed-phase HPLC, the stationary phase is hydrophobic (e.g., silica functionalized with non-polar C18 octadecyl chains), while the mobile phase is polar (water/acetonitrile mixture).
  • Therefore, the stationary phase is less polar than the mobile phase (the reverse of traditional normal-phase chromatography).

question: In ultrafiltration, identify which one of the following relationships between transmembrane pressure (TMP) and flux (F) is CORRECT
options: For water, initially F increases with TMP and remains constant
For water, F always increases with TMP
For water, F always decreases with TMP
For water, initially F decreases with TMP and remains constant
correct_answer: For water, F always increases with TMP
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Ultrafiltration Flux and Transmembrane Pressure (TMP):
  • For pure water in ultrafiltration, Darcy's law holds: $$J_w = \frac{\text{TMP}}{\mu R_m}$$
  • Because there are no solute concentration polarization or fouling layers with pure water, the hydraulic water flux $F$ always increases linearly with Transmembrane Pressure (TMP).

question: Identify the INCORRECT match
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Scientific Contributions in Biology:
  • Louis Pasteur demonstrated the germ theory of disease, disproved spontaneous generation, developed pasteurization, and created rabies/anthrax vaccines. He did not formulate the blood clotting cascade theory.

question: The first smallpox vaccine is an example of
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Jenner's Smallpox Vaccine:
  • Edward Jenner's smallpox vaccine utilized infectious cowpox virus (vaccinia), a replication-competent live virus that provoked robust protective immunity against variola, making it the historic prototype of a live vaccine.

question: ELISPOT assay is traditionally used for measuring
explanation:
[CONCEPT] ELISPOT Assay Application:
  • ELISPOT (Enzyme-Linked ImmunoSpot): Quantifies the frequency of cytokine-secreting T cells (e.g., IFN-$\gamma$-secreting antigen-specific T cells) at single-cell resolution. Each colored spot corresponds to a single cytokine-secreting cell.

question: Fertility factor’ is related to ‘conjugation’ in the same way as ‘bacteriophage P1’ to
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Bacterial Genetic Exchange Mechanisms:
  • The Fertility factor ($F$-plasmid) mediates bacterial conjugation.
  • Similarly, a bacteriophage (bacterial virus) mediates horizontal gene transfer via transduction.

question: Hemorrhage in the brain tissue with loss of consciousness is known as
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Medical Terminology: Apoplexy:
  • Apoplexy: A traditional clinical term referring to sudden neurological impairment and loss of consciousness caused by acute internal hemorrhage or stroke within brain tissue.

question: Which one of the following methods is frequently used to create transgenic animals?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Generation of Transgenic Mice:
  • The most common and established method for generating transgenic mice is pronuclear (nuclear) micro-injection, where purified linear DNA constructs are directly injected into the male pronucleus of a fertilized single-cell zygote.

question: Which of the following is an atypical signaling receptor?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Mannose Receptor as an Atypical Receptor:
  • The Mannose Receptor (CD206) is a C-type lectin that functions primarily as an endocytic pattern-recognition receptor for clearance of pathogens and glycoproteins, lacking classical kinase-associated signaling domains, characterizing it as an atypical receptor.

question: The critical regulatory site in the circuit of emotions is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Neuroanatomy of Emotion: The Amygdala:
  • The Amygdala, located deep in the temporal lobes of the limbic system, is the central regulatory hub for emotional processing, fear conditioning, aggression, and emotional memory consolidation.

question: Which glial cells participate in the re-uptake mechanism of neurotransmitter from the synaptic cleft?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Astrocyte Role in Synaptic Neurotransmitter Re-Uptake:
  • Astrocytes (astroglia) express high levels of excitatory amino acid transporters (EAAT1/GLAST and EAAT2/GLT-1) that rapidly clear neurotransmitters (especially glutamate) from the synaptic cleft, preventing excitotoxicity and recycling neurotransmitters via the glutamate-glutamine cycle.

question: Red data book contains data of ….
explanation:
[CONCEPT] IUCN Red Data Book:
  • The Red Data Book, maintained by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), contains comprehensive documentation and status categories for global threatened and endangered species.

question: Conservation within the natural habitat is ……
explanation:
[CONCEPT] In Situ vs. Ex Situ Conservation:
  • In situ conservation: Conservation of species and ecosystems within their natural habitats (e.g., national parks, biosphere reserves, wildlife sanctuaries).
  • Ex situ conservation: Conservation outside the natural habitat (e.g., botanical gardens, zoological parks, cryopreserved seed banks).

question: MAB program stands for…
explanation:
[CONCEPT] UNESCO MAB Programme:
  • The MAB program stands for UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme, launched in 1971 to promote scientific approaches to balancing biodiversity conservation with sustainable human development.

question: Marine organisms that require oxygen levels typically in the range of 2-10 % for growth would be classed under
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Oxygen Requirements of Microorganisms:
  • Microaerophiles: Organisms that require oxygen for aerobic respiration, but only at low atmospheric partial pressures (typically $2\text{--}10\%\text{ O}_2$), being poisoned by normal atmospheric oxygen concentrations ($21\%\text{ O}_2$).

question: Along which plate boundaries do the majority of the world's earthquakes occur?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Tectonic Plate Boundaries and Earthquakes:
  • Earthquakes occur along divergent, convergent, and transform fault boundaries (such as the San Andreas Fault), where tectonic plates slide horizontally past one another, generating massive shear stress releases.

question: Which of the following will increase the salinity of a particular area of coastal water?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Sea Ice Freezing and Salinity Increase:
  • When seawater freezes to form sea ice, salt is excluded from the forming crystal lattice (a process known as brine rejection). The rejected concentrated brine sinks, markedly increasing the salinity of the surrounding liquid water.

question: An individual has the genotype AaBbccddEe. Assuming independent assortment what frequency of gametes will have the genotype abcde?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Mendelian Gamete Frequency Calculation:
  • Given genotype $AaBbccddEe$:
    • $Aa$ produces gamete allele $a$ with probability $1/2$.
    • $Bb$ produces gamete allele $b$ with probability $1/2$.
    • $cc$ produces allele $c$ with probability $1$.
    • $dd$ produces allele $d$ with probability $1$.
    • $Ee$ produces allele $e$ with probability $1/2$.
  • Probability of gamete $abcde = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 1 \times \frac{1}{2} = \mathbf{\frac{1}{8}}$.

question: If the DNA content of a cell in G1 phase of cell cycle is ‘C’, what will be its content after meiosis is completed?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Meiotic DNA Content Reduction:
  • If the somatic diploid cell DNA content in $G_1$ phase is designated as $C$, the cell duplicates its DNA in $S$ phase to $2C$.
  • Following meiosis I and meiosis II, the four haploid gametes each contain half of the original $G_1$ diploid DNA content, which is $1/2\ C$.

question: Which type of chemical mutagen is incorporated into the genome by DNA polymerase during replication?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Base Analogs as Mutagens:
  • Base Analogs: Chemical mutagens (such as 5-bromouracil and 2-aminopurine) that structurally resemble normal nitrogenous bases. DNA polymerases mistake them for normal nucleotides and incorporate them into the growing DNA strand during replication, leading to transition mutations during subsequent rounds of replication.

question: Which of the following constitutes a necessary and sufficient condition for two proteins to be considered homologous?
options: The sequences of the proteins must show greater than 50% identity in a Global alignment
The sequences of the proteins must show greater than 50% identity in a local alignment
The proteins should have diverged from a common ancestor
The proteins should have very similar structure and function
correct_answer: The proteins should have diverged from a common ancestor
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Definition of Homology in Protein Evolution:
  • Homology: A necessary and sufficient condition for homology is that two proteins share common ancestry (they have diverged from a common ancestral sequence). High sequence identity is evidence for homology, but homology itself is an all-or-nothing evolutionary relationship.

question: Boiling a mixture of butter, water and eggs, results in a homogenous suspension; However if the eggs are omitted, then the butter and the water separate out. Which component, present in the egg, is responsible for this behaviour?
options: Various salts of sodium and magnesium that are present in eggs
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Lecithin as a Food Emulsifier in Egg Yolk:
  • Egg yolk contains abundant amounts of lecithin (phosphatidylcholine), an amphiphilic phospholipid with polar phosphate-choline heads and non-polar fatty acid tails that acts as a natural emulsifier, stabilizing oil-and-water mixtures (like mayonnaise and custard) into homogenous solutions.

question: Cooking meat in presence of cut pieces of Papaya fruit results in unusually tender meat. What enzyme, present in the Papaya fruit is responsible for this?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Papain as a Meat Tenderizer:
  • Papaya fruit contains the cysteine endopeptidase papain, which enzymatically cleaves peptide bonds in tough muscle structural proteins (collagen and actomyosin), resulting in tenderized meat during cooking.

question: Which of the following peptide sequences will match the sequence motif GXX[SVP]XXG?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] PROSITE Motif Matching:
  • The motif P-G-Q-R-V-[GS]-G-G-R requires: $$P - G - Q - R - V - (G \text{ or } S) - G - G - R$$
  • The peptide sequence PGQRVGGGR contains Glycine ($G$) at the variable position 6, perfectly matching the consensus signature.

question: In Mass Spectroscopy, a qudrupole mass filter does which of the following?
options: It makes possible the detection of four times larger ions than normal.
It specifically filters out those complex ions that have two positive and two negative charges.
It specifically allows ions with two positive and two negative charges and blocks the rest.
It allows only those ions which have a specific m/z ratio to pass through.
correct_answer: It allows only those ions which have a specific m/z ratio to pass through.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Principles of Quadrupole Mass Analyzers:
  • A quadrupole mass filter consists of four parallel hyperbolic molybdenum rods. By applying specific ratios of radio-frequency (RF) and direct-current (DC) voltages, an oscillating electric field is generated that creates stable resonant trajectories only for ions of a specific mass-to-charge ratio ($m/z$), allowing them to pass through to the detector while all other ions collide with the rods and are neutralized.

question: If maltose and monosodium glutamate (MSG) are added to a vinegar and palmitic acid and shaken, the mixture will eventually separate into two phases of different density and polarity. Where will most of the sucrose and the MSG be located following phase separation?
options: Both will concentrate in the vinegar.
Both will concentrate in the oil.
Maltose will concentrate in the oil and MSG will concentrate in the vinegar.
Maltose will concentrate in the vinegar and MSG will concentrate in the oil.
correct_answer: Both will concentrate in the vinegar.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Phase Partitioning in Biphasic Food Systems (Oil and Vinegar):
  • A salad dressing of oil and vinegar forms a two-phase liquid mixture consisting of an aqueous, polar phase (vinegar, dilute acetic acid in water) and an organic, non-polar phase (vegetable oil, hydrophobic triglycerides).
  • Maltose: A hydrophilic disaccharide consisting of two glucose units rich in polar hydroxyl ($-OH$) groups that form extensive hydrogen bonds with water.
  • Monosodium Glutamate (MSG): An ionic salt of glutamic acid ($Na^+$ and glutamate ion) that is highly water-soluble and completely insoluble in non-polar lipid matrices.
  • Because both maltose and MSG are polar and hydrophilic, neither will partition into the hydrophobic oil phase; both will concentrate in the vinegar (aqueous) phase.

question: A slide of macrophage was stained by immunofluorescence using a monoclonal antibody for TAP1/TAP2 complex. Which of the following intracellular compartments would exhibit positive staining with this antibody?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Intracellular Localization of Calreticulin:
  • Calreticulin: A high-capacity calcium-binding molecular chaperone located primarily within the lumen of the Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER).
  • Together with calnexin, calreticulin forms the calreticulin/calnexin quality-control cycle that transiently binds monoglucosylated $N$-glycans on newly synthesized glycoproteins, ensuring correct tertiary folding before export to the Golgi.
  • Therefore, immunofluorescence staining with an anti-calreticulin monoclonal antibody highlights the endoplasmic reticulum.

question: Which of the following disorder is not X-linked?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genetics of Sex-Linked Disorders vs. Swyer Syndrome:
  • X-Linked Disorders: Hemophilia A/B, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Red-green color blindness, and Fragile X syndrome are classic $X$-linked traits caused by mutations on the $X$ chromosome.
  • Swyer Syndrome (Pure Gonadal Dysgenesis, 46,XY): Affected individuals have a male karyotype ($46,XY$) but a female external phenotype with streak gonads. It is caused predominantly by loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the $SRY$ gene located on the $Y$ chromosome (or mutations in autosomal genes like $SOX9$ or $NR5A1$). It is NOT an X-linked disorder.

question: α-amanitin inhibits
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Differential Sensitivity of Eukaryotic RNA Polymerases to $\alpha$-Amanitin:
  • $\alpha$-Amanitin: A deadly bicyclic octapeptide toxin produced by the death cap mushroom Amanita phalloides that blocks mRNA elongation.
  • Enzyme Sensitivities:
    • RNA Polymerase II (synthesizes mRNA, snRNA): Extremely sensitive; inhibited at very low concentrations ($10^{-8}\text{ M}$ or $\sim 1\ \mu\text{g/mL}$).
    • RNA Polymerase III (synthesizes tRNA, 5S rRNA): Moderately sensitive; inhibited only at high concentrations ($10^{-6}\text{ M}$).
    • RNA Polymerase I (synthesizes large 28S, 18S, 5.8S rRNAs): Completely insensitive / resistant.
  • Therefore, $\alpha$-amanitin specifically inhibits RNA polymerase II.

question: Nullisomy is the term used for the condition when an organism has
options: Loss of one homologous pair of chromosome
correct_answer: Loss of one homologous pair of chromosome
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Aneuploidy Terminology:
  • Monosomy ($2n - 1$): Loss of a single individual chromosome.
  • Trisomy ($2n + 1$): Addition of an extra individual chromosome.
  • Nullisomy ($2n - 2$): The loss of an entire pair of homologous chromosomes. Both copies of a specific chromosome are missing from the somatic diploid complement.

question: Tunicamycin blocks
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Tunicamycin Inhibition of Protein Glycosylation:
  • Tunicamycin: An analog of UDP-$N$-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc).
  • Mechanism of Action: It specifically inhibits the enzyme UDP-N-acetylglucosamine:dolichyl-phosphate N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphate transferase (GPT / DPAGT1), which catalyzes the transfer of GlcNAc-1-P onto dolichol phosphate—the very first committed step in assembling the lipid-linked core oligosaccharide ($Glc_3Man_9GlcNAc_2\text{-PP-Dol}$) in the ER.
  • By blocking the synthesis of the lipid-linked precursor, tunicamycin completely blocks $N$-linked glycosylation of proteins.

question: Which of the following cannot be used in finding the interaction between miRNA and mRNA?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Techniques for Protein-Protein vs. Protein-RNA Interactions:
  • Yeast two-hybrid, co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), and Far-Western blotting are standard methods used to detect physical protein-protein interactions.
  • PAR-CLIP (Photoactivatable-Ribonucleoside-Enhanced Crosslinking and Immunoprecipitation): A high-throughput sequencing method developed to map protein-RNA interactions and identify binding sites of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) or microRNA-protein complexes. It is not designed to find protein-protein interactions.

question: H1N1, H1N2, H2N1, H3N1 and H3N2 are subtypes of which influenza virus?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Subtypes of Influenza A Viruses:
  • Influenza viruses belong to the family Orthomyxoviridae.
  • Only Influenza A viruses are classified into antigenic subtypes based on the combination of their two surface glycoproteins: Hemagglutinin ($H$, 18 subtypes, H1–H18) and Neuraminidase ($N$, 11 subtypes, N1–N11).
  • Hence, subtypes like H1N1, H1N2, H2N1, H3N1, and H3N2 all belong strictly to Influenza A.

question: A mother and a father, both CF (cystic fibrosis) carriers, have two children that do not suffer from CF. The probability of a third pregnancy producing a child with the disease is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Probability of Carrier Offspring in Autosomal Recessive Disorders:
  • Parents: Both mother and father are carriers for cystic fibrosis ($Cc \times Cc$).
  • Offspring Genotypes: $$Cc \times Cc \longrightarrow 1\, CC : 2\, Cc : 1\, cc$$
  • Probability that an individual child is affected ($cc$) is $1/4$, and probability of being a carrier ($Cc$) is $1/2$.
  • Depending on the specific wording of the ratio requested in the question (e.g. probability that both children are affected: $(1/4) \times (1/4) = 1/16$, or single child probability ratio), the evaluated probability corresponds to the 1:4 option.

question: The overall reaction catalyzed by the electron transport chain is
options: NADH + H+ + ½ O 2 → NAD+ + H2O
correct_answer: NADH + H+ + ½ O 2 → NAD+ + H2O
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Overall Bioenergetics of Mitochondrial Electron Transport Chain:
  • Electrons from reduced coenzyme NADH enter Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), pass through ubiquinone, Complex III (cytochrome $bc_1$), cytochrome $c$, and Complex IV (cytochrome $c$ oxidase), where molecular oxygen serves as the terminal electron acceptor.
  • Net Overall Stoichiometric Reaction: $$\mathbf{NADH + H^+ + \frac{1}{2} O_2 \longrightarrow NAD^+ + H_2O}$$
  • This exergonic oxidation ($Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -220\text{ kJ/mol}$) drives proton translocation across the inner mitochondrial membrane to generate the proton-motive force for ATP synthesis.

question: DNA polymerase III of E. coli is
options: required for de novo synthesis of new strands of DNA
involved in the repair of damaged DNA
required to restart a replication fork
correct_answer: required for de novo synthesis of new strands of DNA
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Functions of E. coli DNA Polymerase III:
  • DNA Polymerase III: The primary replicative holoenzyme in E. coli.
  • It possesses high processivity ($>1000\text{ nt/s}$) conferred by the $\beta$-sliding clamp, and is responsible for the continuous de novo synthesis/elongation of the leading strand and discontinuous elongation of Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
  • (DNA Polymerase I removes RNA primers and fills gaps; DNA Pol II, IV, and V function in translesion synthesis and DNA repair).

question: The protection against smallpox afforded by prior infection with cowpox represents
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Edward Jenner and Antigenic Cross-Reactivity:
  • In 1796, Edward Jenner observed that milkmaids who contracted mild cowpox lesions were immune to lethal smallpox.
  • Mechanism: Cowpox virus (vaccinia) shares structurally homologous surface antigens and epitopes with variola virus (smallpox). Antibodies and memory lymphocytes elicited by cowpox recognize and neutralize variola virus due to antigenic cross-reactivity.

question: Internalized antigens are targeted to which of the following compartments for generation of appropriate peptide for presentation on the cell surface along with MHC molecule
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Lysosomal Degradation of Endocytosed Antigens:
  • In the exogenous pathway of antigen presentation, antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) internalize extracellular antigens by endocytosis or phagocytosis.
  • The internalized vesicles fuse with endosomes and mature into acidic lysosomes (phagolysosomes), where lysosomal acid hydrolases (cathepsins B, D, L, S) degrade the foreign antigens into immunogenic peptides for loading onto MHC Class II molecules.

question: In which receptor system, both receptor and ligand are recycled back to membrane
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Receptor and Ligand Recycling in the Transferrin Cycle:
  • In the transferrin cycle, diferric transferrin ($Fe_2\text{-Tf}$) binds the transferrin receptor (TfR) at neutral physiological pH ($7.4$) and undergoes clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
  • Inside acidic early endosomes (pH $\sim 5.5$), iron is released from transferrin, but apotransferrin (iron-free transferrin) remains tightly bound to TfR at this low pH.
  • The entire receptor-ligand complex is recycled back to the plasma membrane. Upon encountering the neutral extracellular pH of the blood, apotransferrin dissociates from TfR to bind fresh iron, while TfR is ready for another round of endocytosis. Thus, both receptor and ligand are recycled!

question: GTP binding proteins are active in GTP bound form. Which of the following protein coverts the GTP bound form to GDP bound form.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Regulation of Monomeric Small GTPases:
  • Small G-proteins (Ras, Rho, Rab, Ran) cycle between an active GTP-bound state and an inactive GDP-bound state.
  • GTPase-Activating Proteins (GAPs): Bind to the active GTPase and dramatically accelerate its intrinsic GTP hydrolysis rate by up to $10^5$-fold, stimulating the conversion of active GTP-bound G-protein into the inactive GDP-bound form (turning the molecular switch OFF).
  • (Guanine Nucleotide Exchange Factors, GEFs, do the opposite: they promote GDP release and GTP binding to activate the switch).

question: Which enzyme is used to remove the phosphate group from 5' end of the DNA?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Role of Alkaline Phosphatase in Recombinant DNA Technology:
  • Alkaline Phosphatase (CIP / BAP): Catalyzes the hydrolytic removal of the $5'$-phosphate group from DNA and RNA strands, leaving a $5'$-hydroxyl ($-OH$) group.
  • In molecular cloning, treating a linearized plasmid vector with alkaline phosphatase prevents vector self-ligation (recircularization) because DNA ligase strictly requires a $5'$-phosphate and a $3'$-hydroxyl to form a phosphodiester bond.

question: Which one of the following techniques is suitable for the large scale purification of isozymes (A and B) that are differing from each other by a single positive charged amino acid?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chromatofocusing for Protein Separation:
  • Chromatofocusing: A high-resolution column chromatographic method that separates amphoteric biomolecules (proteins) based on differences in their isoelectric points (pI).
  • An anion-exchange column is equilibrated at a high pH, and a specialized amphoteric buffering system (Polybuffer) at a lower pH is passed through it. As the buffer moves through the column, an internally generated linear pH gradient develops, causing each protein to migrate and focus sharply into narrow zones where the local pH equals its pI.

question: Glycogen and cellulose are
options: Helical structures but with different degree of helicity
Helical but glycogen is extensively branched molecule
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Conformational Architecture of Glycogen and Cellulose:
  • Glycogen: Composed of D-glucose units linked by $\alpha(1\to4)$ bonds with frequent $\alpha(1\to6)$ branches. The bent geometry of $\alpha(1\to4)$ glycosidic linkages causes the polysaccharide chain to adopt a compact, coiled helical conformation ideal for rapid mobilization as an energy store.
  • Cellulose: Composed of D-glucose units joined by $\beta(1\to4)$ linkages. The $\beta$ linkage allows adjacent glucose residues to flip $180^\circ$ relative to each other, forming a rigid, straight, extended chain that packs side-by-side into parallel sheet-like / microfibrillar structures stabilized by intra- and inter-molecular hydrogen bonds.

question: Which one of the following factors influences the binding of oxygen to hemoglobin?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation:
  • The primary physiological determinant of hemoglobin saturation is the partial pressure of oxygen ($P_{\text{O}_2}$).
  • As $P_{\text{O}_2}$ rises, positive cooperativity between hemoglobin's four heme subunits facilitates oxygen binding, producing the classic sigmoidal oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. (Secondary allosteric regulators include $P_{\text{CO}_2}$, pH, temperature, and 2,3-BPG).

question: Which one of the following DNA viruses has part of its life cycle involving Reverse Transcriptase enzyme, which is a hallmark of Retroviruses?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Hepatitis B Virus and Reverse Transcription:
  • Hepatitis B Virus (HBV): A pararetrovirus (family Hepadnaviridae) possessing a circular, partially double-stranded relaxed DNA genome (rcDNA).
  • Life Cycle: Inside the hepatocyte nucleus, the viral DNA is repaired into covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), which is transcribed by host RNA polymerase II into a pregenomic RNA (pgRNA) intermediate. Viral reverse transcriptase (P protein) then reverse-transcribes the pgRNA into new viral DNA during capsidation in the cytoplasm.

question: Cells are broken to release the contents by using various enzymes. Which of the following combination is FALSE?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Cell Wall Lysis Enzyme Specificity:
  • Cellulase: Specifically hydrolyzes $\beta(1\to4)$ glycosidic bonds in cellulose found in plant cell walls (and certain algae/oomycetes). Bacteria possess peptidoglycan cell walls (cleaved by lysozyme), NOT cellulose. Therefore, Cellulase – bacteria is an incorrect match.

question: Which of the following enzymes is required to release the tension imposed by uncoiling of strands?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Role of DNA Gyrase in Replication:
  • As the replicative helicase (DnaB) unwinds the double helix at the replication fork, positive supercoiling and extreme torsional stress build up in the unreplicated DNA ahead of the fork.
  • DNA Gyrase (Topoisomerase II): Cleaves both strands of duplex DNA, passes another duplex segment through the break, and reseals it, introducing negative supercoils and releasing the torsional tension, preventing the replication fork from stalling.

question: DNA fingerprinting is based on
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Principles of DNA Fingerprinting:
  • DNA profiling / fingerprinting (invented by Sir Alec Jeffreys in 1984) is based on the detection of polymorphism in Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTRs / Minisatellites).
  • These hypervariable repeated DNA loci differ in repeat copy number among individuals, producing unique restriction fragment length profiles upon Southern hybridization or PCR amplification.

question: The DNA sequence is ATG. What would be the sequence of bases in anticodon of tRNA
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genetic Code, mRNA Codon, and tRNA Anticodon:
  • Given coding DNA strand: $5'\text{-ATG-}3'$.
  • The transcribed mRNA codon is: $5'\text{-AUG-}3'$ (methionine start codon).
  • The cognate tRNA anticodon base-pairs antiparallel to the mRNA: $$\text{mRNA (5' to 3'): } \mathbf{A - U - G}$$ $$\text{tRNA (3' to 5'): } \mathbf{U - A - C}$$
  • Writing the anticodon in standard $5'\to3'$ notation: $\mathbf{5'\text{-CAU-}3'}$.

question: All except one of the following are true about the protein kinase A (PKA) pathway
options: PKA phosphorylates proteins at serine or threonine residues
PKA phosphorylates proteins at tyrosine residues
PKA is activated by binding of epinephrine to a transmembrane receptor without enzyme activity
correct_answer: PKA phosphorylates proteins at tyrosine residues
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Protein Kinase A (PKA) Signaling Characteristics:
  • PKA: A cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase that functions downstream of $G_s$-coupled GPCRs (such as the $\beta$-adrenergic receptor responding to epinephrine).
  • Binding of cAMP to the regulatory subunits of PKA releases the active catalytic subunits.
  • PKA is a classic Serine/Threonine kinase that transfers the $\gamma$-phosphate of ATP to serine or threonine residues within the consensus motif $\text{Arg-Arg-X-Ser/Thr}$. It does NOT phosphorylate proteins at tyrosine residues (tyrosine phosphorylation is mediated by tyrosine kinases like Src or EGFR).

question: A T- cytotoxic cell can be induced to mount a cytotoxic attack on a virus-infected cell if it binds to a cell displaying
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Cytotoxic T Lymphocyte (CTL) Target Recognition:
  • $CD8^+$ cytotoxic T cells recognize intracellular antigens (such as viral peptides) presented in the peptide-binding cleft of MHC Class I molecules on the surface of target cells.
  • Binding of the T-cell receptor (TCR) and CD8 coreceptor to the MHC I-foreign peptide complex activates the CTL to release perforin and granzymes, inducing target cell apoptosis.

question: Testosterone hormone, necessary for spermatogenesis, is secreted by
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Endocrine Function of Leydig Cells:
  • In the mammalian testes, interstitial Leydig cells located in the connective tissue between seminiferous tubules synthesize and secrete the steroid hormone testosterone in response to Luteinizing Hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary.
  • Testosterone acts locally on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis and maintains male secondary sexual characteristics.

question: Which of the following processes occurs in the formation of disulfide bridge between two cystiene residues?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chemistry of Disulfide Bond Formation:
  • A disulfide bond (cystine bridge) is a covalent linkage formed between the thiol ($-SH$) sulfhydryl groups of two cysteine residues: $$2\,\text{R-SH} \xrightarrow{\text{Oxidation}} \text{R-S-S-R} + 2\,\text{H}^+ + 2\,\text{e}^-$$
  • This is an oxidation reaction (loss of electrons and hydrogen atoms) catalyzed in vivo by protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) in the endoplasmic reticulum.

question: In Ramachandran plot, the values of the dihedral angle ψ (psi) is based on rotation around
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Ramachandran Plot Dihedral Angles:
  • The conformation of a protein backbone is defined by three torsional dihedral angles per amino acid residue:
    • $\mathbf{\phi\text{ (phi):}}$ Rotation around the $N - C_\alpha$ bond.
    • $\mathbf{\psi\text{ (psi):}}$ Rotation around the $\mathbf{C_\alpha - C'}$ bond (between alpha carbon and carbonyl carbon).
    • $\omega\text{ (omega):}$ Rotation around the peptide bond ($C' - N$, usually fixed at $180^\circ$ trans).
  • Therefore, $\psi$ is based on rotation around the $C_\alpha - C'$ bond.

question: Which one of the following antibiotics attaches to 50S ribosome and inhibits peptidyl- transferase activity?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Mechanism of Action of Chloramphenicol:
  • Chloramphenicol: Binds specifically to the 50S ribosomal subunit near the peptidyl transferase center, sterically blocking peptide bond formation between peptidyl-tRNA and aminoacyl-tRNA.
  • Note on Exam Answer Key: The official question paper key erroneously designated Option 3 (Trimethoprim, which actually inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase). Pharmacologically and biochemically, the correct answer is Chloramphenicol.

question: The cytological representation of Klinefelter syndrome is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Karyotype of Klinefelter Syndrome:
  • Klinefelter Syndrome: A common sex chromosome aneuploidy in males caused by meiotic non-disjunction, resulting in an extra $X$ chromosome.
  • The cytogenetic formula is $47,XXY$, consisting of 22 pairs of normal autosomes (44 autosomes, $44A$) plus three sex chromosomes ($XXY$): $\mathbf{44A + XXY}$.

question: A chromosome on which T-cell receptor alpha chain gene rearrangement has occurred lacks which of the following gene segments?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Gene Rearrangement in T-Cell Receptor $\alpha$ Chain:
  • The human TCR $\alpha$ chain gene locus (like immunoglobulin light chain loci $\kappa$ and $\lambda$) consists only of Variable ($V$), Joining ($J$), and Constant ($C$) segments.
  • It lacks Diversity ($D$) gene segments! ($D$ segments are present only in TCR $\beta$, TCR $\delta$, and immunoglobulin heavy chain loci). Rearrangement involves $V_\alpha$ directly joining to $J_\alpha$.

question: Which one of the following molecule yields higher amount of free energy?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] High-Energy Phosphate Compounds and Free Energy of Hydrolysis:
  • Standard free energies of hydrolysis ($\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$):
    • Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP): $\mathbf{-61.9\text{ kJ/mol}}$ ($-14.8\text{ kcal/mol}$)
    • 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate: $-49.3\text{ kJ/mol}$
    • Phosphocreatine: $-43.0\text{ kJ/mol}$
    • ATP (to ADP + Pi): $-30.5\text{ kJ/mol}$ ($-7.3\text{ kcal/mol}$)
    • Glucose-6-phosphate: $-13.8\text{ kJ/mol}$
  • Phosphoenolpyruvate yields the highest standard free energy of hydrolysis among common metabolic intermediates, driving substrate-level phosphorylation of ADP to ATP in pyruvate kinase.

question: Which region of mRNA contains Shine-Dalgarno sequence?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Prokaryotic Ribosome Binding Site (Shine-Dalgarno Sequence):
  • In bacteria, translation initiation requires positioning of the 30S ribosomal subunit at the start codon.
  • The Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequence is a purine-rich consensus sequence (typically $5'\text{-AGGAGG-}3'$) located in the $5'$ untranslated region ($5'$ UTR) of the mRNA, about $7\text{--}10$ nucleotides upstream of the AUG initiation codon. It base-pairs with the complementary anti-Shine-Dalgarno sequence at the $3'$-end of 16S rRNA.

question: α-D glucose and β-D glucose are
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Anomers of D-Glucose:
  • When D-glucose cyclizes from its open-chain form into a six-membered pyranose ring, the planar carbonyl carbon (C1) becomes a new chiral stereocenter called the anomeric carbon.
  • Two cyclic diastereomers are formed:
    • $\alpha$-D-glucose: Hydroxyl group at C1 is in the trans / axial (downward) position relative to the $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group at C5.
    • $\beta$-D-glucose: Hydroxyl group at C1 is in the cis / equatorial (upward) position.
  • Stereoisomers that differ in configuration only at the anomeric hemiacetal carbon are defined as anomers.

question: Which of the following statements is NOT true for eukaryotic DNA replication?
options: It is synchronized to phases of cell cycle
It does not involve Okazaki fragment
It requires licencing of Pre-replicative complex
correct_answer: It does not involve Okazaki fragment
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Discontinuous Lagging Strand Synthesis in Eukaryotes:
  • Because DNA polymerases synthesize DNA exclusively in the $5'\to3'$ direction, the lagging strand template must be copied discontinuously.
  • In both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, lagging strand synthesis produces short RNA-primed DNA segments known as Okazaki fragments (about $100\text{--}200$ nucleotides long in eukaryotes, synthesized by DNA Polymerase $\delta$). Therefore, the claim that eukaryotic replication does not involve Okazaki fragments is NOT true.

question: In vitro characterization of E. coli DNA polymerase shows an error rate of 10 -6 -10-7 per base pair. However, in vivo, the observed mutation rate is 10-9 -10 -10 per base. Such discrepancy is because:
options: In vitro assays for DNA polymerase is less precise than in vivo assays.
E. coli has a mechanism of removing such erroneous incorporation of bases.
The mechanism by which DNA polymerase amplifies linear DNA used in vitro is different from that of circular DNA in vivo.
The reason for such discrepancy is not known yet.
correct_answer: E. coli has a mechanism of removing such erroneous incorporation of bases.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Proofreading and Mismatch Repair in E. coli:
  • Although purified DNA polymerase III incorporates mispaired nucleotides at an in vitro error rate of $\sim 10^{-4}$ to $10^{-5}$, the observed in vivo mutation rate of E. coli is vastly lower ($sim 10^{-9}$ to $10^{-10}$).
  • This fidelity is achieved because E. coli has multiple layers of post-replicative surveillance: its own intrinsic $3'\to5'$ exonucleolytic proofreading domain and the post-replication Mismatch Repair (MMR) system that recognizes and removes misincorporated bases.

question: The molecular formulae of deoxyribose sugar and ribose sugar, respectively, are
options: C5 H10 O 4 and C 5 H10 O 6
C5 H10 O 4 and C 5 H10 O 5
C5 H10 O 5 and C 5 H10 O 4
C5 H10 O 5 and C 6 H10 O 4
correct_answer: C5 H10 O 4 and C 5 H10 O 5
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chemical Formulas of Ribose and Deoxyribose:
  • Ribose: A normal aldopentose sugar with five oxygen atoms: $\mathbf{C_5 H_{10} O_5}$.
  • 2-Deoxyribose: Derived from ribose by replacing the hydroxyl group at the C2 position with a hydrogen atom (lacking one oxygen atom): $\mathbf{C_5 H_{10} O_4}$.

question: Usually intracellular pathogens avoid their transport to lysosome for their survival in the host cell. But which of the following intracellular pathogens survives in the lysosomes?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Intracellular Survival of Leishmania within Phagolysosomes:
  • Most intracellular bacteria and parasites (such as Mycobacterium, Legionella, and Toxoplasma) survive inside host cells by actively inhibiting phagosome-lysosome fusion.
  • In contrast, the protozoan parasite Leishmania (in its intracellular amastigote form inside macrophages) uniquely thrives and multiplies directly inside mature, fully acidified phagolysosomes, utilizing specialized surface lipophosphoglycans (LPG) and acid phosphatases to resist lysosomal acid hydrolases.

question: When Hfr strain of E. coli is crossed with F- strain, recombinant obtained are
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genetics of Hfr $\times$ F- Bacterial Conjugation:
  • In an High-Frequency Recombination (Hfr) strain, the $F$ (fertility) factor is integrated into the host bacterial chromosome.
  • During conjugation with an $F^-$ recipient, chromosomal transfer initiates at the origin of transfer (oriT) within the integrated $F$ plasmid and proceeds linearly around the bacterial chromosome. The remainder of the $F$ factor sequence is transferred last.
  • Because transferring the entire E. coli chromosome takes $\sim 100\text{ minutes}$, conjugation bridges almost always rupture prematurely due to brownian agitation, so the complete $F$ plasmid is rarely transferred. Consequently, the recipient recombinant almost always remains $F^-$ (rarely becomes $F^+$).

question: Archea is considered as a separate group from bacteria and eukaryotes, based on
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Carl Woese's Three-Domain System Based on 16S rRNA:
  • In 1977, Carl Woese and George Fox revolutionized biological taxonomy by comparing nucleotide sequences of the 16S ribosomal RNA (16S rRNA) gene across diverse organisms.
  • They discovered that methanogens and extreme halophiles/thermophiles differed as profoundly from standard bacteria as they did from eukaryotes, leading to the classification of life into three distinct evolutionary domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eucarya.

question: How many grams of NaCl will be required to make 10 ml of 10 millimolar solution (MW of NaCl = 58.5)
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Mass of NaCl Required for a Millimolar Solution:
  • Given:
    • Volume ($V$) = $10\text{ mL} = 0.01\text{ L}$
    • Molarity ($M$) = $10\text{ mM} = 10 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M} = 0.01\text{ mol/L}$
    • Molar mass of NaCl = $58.44\text{ g/mol}$
  • Calculation: $$\text{Moles } (n) = M \times V = 0.01\text{ mol/L} \times 0.01\text{ L} = 10^{-4}\text{ moles}$$ $$\text{Mass } (m) = n \times MW = 10^{-4}\text{ mol} \times 58.44\text{ g/mol} = \mathbf{0.005844\text{ g} \approx 0.00585\text{ g}}$$

question: Keratin intermediate filaments are synthesized in the cytoplasm of cells. Disulfide bonds cannot be formed in the cytoplasm. However, the keratin fibers in the skin are cross-linked by disulfide bonds. This is because
options: Keratin fibers get transported via endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi to the skin surface
Keratin crosslinking happens in dead cells whose contents are oxidized
Secreted enzymes of the skin cells form the disulfide bonds after secretion of keratin fibers
correct_answer: Keratin crosslinking happens in dead cells whose contents are oxidized
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Disulfide Crosslinking of Keratin in Cornified Cells:
  • In living epithelial cells (stratum basale and spinosum), the cytoplasm is maintaining a reducing environment with high glutathione (GSH) levels, keeping cysteine sulfhydryl ($-SH$) groups reduced and preventing uncontrolled disulfide bonding.
  • As keratinocytes migrate to the surface (stratum corneum), they undergo programmed cell death (cornification) and lose metabolic control. Exposure to atmospheric oxygen and loss of reducing machinery creates an oxidized state where keratin intermediate filaments form massive networks of covalent disulfide crosslinks, producing the rigid, water-resistant stratum corneum.

question: Which of the following plays a role in changing the antigen binding site of a B cell after antigenic stimulation?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Affinity Maturation and Somatic Hypermutation:
  • Somatic Hypermutation (SHM): Occurs in the germinal centers of secondary lymphoid organs after B-cell activation by antigen.
  • The enzyme AID introduces point mutations into the rearranged $V(D)J$ exons of immunoglobulin heavy and light chains at an extraordinary rate ($sim 10^{-3}$ per base per generation).
  • Follicular dendritic cells select B cells with higher affinity for antigen, driving affinity maturation and fine-tuning the antigen-binding specificity of the antibody.

question: What region of an mRNA is most commonly associated with transcript destabilization?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] mRNA 3' UTR and Transcript Stability:
  • The $3'$ untranslated region ($3'$ UTR) of eukaryotic mRNAs contains key sequence motifs that regulate mRNA longevity and decay.
  • These include AU-rich elements (AREs) that recruit deadenylases (such as CCR4-NOT) and target transcripts for rapid exonucleolytic degradation, as well as binding sites for microRNAs (miRNAs) that mediate translational repression and mRNA destabilization.

question: Which type of replication requires a break in the nucleotide strand to get started?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Mechanism of Rolling Circle Replication:
  • Rolling Circle Replication: Utilized by certain bacteriophages ($Phi X174$, M13), plasmids (ColE1 derivatives), and viroids.
  • Replication begins when a sequence-specific endonuclease introduces a single-strand cleavage (a nick or break in one nucleotide strand) at the origin of replication ($dso$), creating a free $3'-OH$ group. DNA polymerase III extends this $3'-OH$ end, displacing the intact $5'$-tail as a single strand while rolling around the circular template.

question: Mismatch repair in bacteria distinguishes between old and new strands of DNA on the basis of
options: Differences in base composition of the two strands
Base analogs on the new strand
Methyl groups on the old strand
correct_answer: Methyl groups on the old strand
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Strand Discrimination in Bacterial Mismatch Repair:
  • Following DNA replication in E. coli, DNA adenine methyltransferase (Dam methylase) methylates the adenine base within $5'\text{-GATC-}3'$ palindromes.
  • Immediately after replication, there is a short temporal lag before the newly synthesized daughter strand is methylated, creating a transient hemimethylated DNA state.
  • The mismatch repair endonuclease MutH binds hemimethylated GATC sites and specifically cleaves the unmethylated daughter strand, directing the repair machinery to replace the error on the new strand while preserving the sequence of the methylated parental strand.

question: Why does the Environmental Protection Agency closely monitors the release of transgenic bacteria used for agricultural purposes?
options: They want to monitor the destruction of crops by the GMOs
They want to observe the effect the GMOs have on crops
They want to ensure the GMOs do not proliferate in the environment and pose a threat to humans
They want to ensure that people are aware that GMOs may have played a role in the production of a particular food product
correct_answer: They want to ensure the GMOs do not proliferate in the environment and pose a threat to humans
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Regulation of GMOs:
  • The release of Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs), particularly transgenic plants producing plant-incorporated protectants (PIPs, like Bt crops) and engineered microorganisms for bioremediation, is closely monitored by regulatory bodies like the EPA.
  • The primary regulatory goal is to prevent ecological disruptions (such as gene flow to weedy relatives, horizontal gene transfer, harm to non-target wildlife) and ensure that recombinant organisms do not persist uncontrollably in the environment or pose toxicological threats to human health.

question: Which of the following events occurs first in the differentiation sequence of human B cells in the bone marrow?
options: Surface IgD and IgM present on the B cell
Surface IgM present on the B cell
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Sequential Order of Antigen Receptor Gene Rearrangement:
  • During B lymphopoiesis in the bone marrow, immunoglobulin gene assembly occurs in a strict, hierarchical developmental program:
    1. Early Pro-B Cell: Rearrangement of the immunoglobulin heavy chain begins with $D_H$ to $J_H$ gene segment joining.
    2. Late Pro-B Cell: $V_H$ joins to $DJ_H$ to complete the functional heavy-chain variable region.
    3. Pre-B Cell: Heavy chain pairs with surrogate light chains ($VpreB$ and $lambda_5$) to form the pre-BCR, signaling the cell to initiate light-chain ($kappa$, then $lambda$) gene rearrangement.
  • Therefore, immunoglobulin heavy chain rearrangement occurs first.

question: A zoo blot helps to detect DNA sequences that
options: Are mutating at a fast rate.
Are lost due to species extinction.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] The Zoo Blot Technique:
  • Zoo Blot: A comparative Southern blot experiment in which genomic DNA samples isolated from a wide variety of phylogenetically diverse animal species (e.g., human, mouse, chicken, frog, fish, fly) are digested, electrophoresed, and hybridized with a specific cloned DNA probe under low-to-moderate stringency.
  • Purpose: Hybridization signals across multiple divergent taxa indicate that the probe contains DNA sequences that are evolutionarily conserved, strongly suggesting that the region corresponds to an essential functional gene or coding exon rather than non-functional junk DNA.

question: Addition of which of the following can prevent the precocious germination of the embryos during embryo culture?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Prevention of Precocious Germination in Somatic Embryogenesis:
  • Precocious Germination: The premature, abnormal sprouting of somatic embryos into weak plantlets before undergoing proper morphological maturation, reserve accumulation, and acquisition of desiccation tolerance.
  • Osmotic Regulation: Inclusion of osmotic agents (such as high concentrations of sucrose, mannitol, or sorbitol) in the maturation medium maintains high osmotic pressure, simulating the natural physiological conditions inside the seed coat. This osmotic constraint, together with abscisic acid (ABA), prevents premature elongation and promotes normal embryo maturation.

question: Which of the following techniques can be used to create diploid homozygous plants in a short span (few months to a year)?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Doubled Haploid Production via Anther Culture:
  • Anther / Microspore Culture (Androgenesis): Involves culturing immature anthers containing uninucleate microspores. Under suitable in vitro hormonal cues, pollen grains undergo androgenesis to develop into haploid ($n$) plants.
  • Diploid Homozygotes (Doubled Haploids): Treating haploid plantlets with the spindle inhibitor colchicine causes chromosome doubling without cytokinesis, producing fertile diploid homozygous ($2n$) plants that are $100\%$ homozygous at every single genetic locus in a single generation!

question: In plant tissue culture experiments, “conditioned medium” refers to a medium in which
options: all the nutrients are added in optimum concentration
all the nutrients are added in high concentration for luxuriant growth
media in which the plant cells have been grown for about 48 hrs and cells are filtered out
plant cells have been grown for about 48 hrs and new cell cultures are added to it.
correct_answer: media in which the plant cells have been grown for about 48 hrs and cells are filtered out
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Conditioned Medium in Plant Cell Suspension Cultures:
  • The Minimum Inoculum Density Effect: In plant tissue culture, isolated single cells or cells plated at very low densities fail to divide and perish because essential diffusible mitogens and growth factors dilute out into the surrounding medium.
  • Conditioned Medium: Medium in which actively dividing plant suspension cells have been grown for about 48 hours and then filtered out to remove the cells. This conditioned medium is enriched with endogenous low-molecular-weight metabolites, amino acids, and cytokines that enable single cells to initiate cell division.

question: An intron containing β-glucuronidase (gus-intron) is used as a reporter gene to assess plant transformation. The intron is introduced to:
options: prevent any expression in the bacterial cells
use it as a target for in situ hybridization for spatial localization of the transcript
correct_answer: prevent any expression in the bacterial cells
explanation:
[CONCEPT] The GUS-Intron Chimeric Reporter Gene:
  • Background: In Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated plant transformation, residual bacteria surviving in intercellular spaces can express reporter genes and give false-positive results.
  • GUS-Plus / GUS-Intron: A plant intron (e.g., from the castor bean catalase gene) is inserted into the coding sequence of the $\beta$-glucuronidase (uidA) gene.
  • Species Specificity: Bacteria lack spliceosomes and cannot excise introns; their ribosomes read into the intron and encounter premature stop codons, preventing any GUS expression in bacterial cells. In contrast, eukaryotic plant cells splice out the intron to produce functional GUS enzyme, ensuring that blue staining reflects bona fide plant transformation.

question: Which one of the following is true about epigenetic changes?
options: Changes are caused by deletion and are heritable
Changes are caused by mutation and are heritable
Changes are caused by mutation but are not heritable
Changes are caused by DNA methylation and are heritable
correct_answer: Changes are caused by DNA methylation and are heritable
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Epigenetic Modifications and Mitotic/Meiotic Heritability:
  • Epigenetics: Refers to stable, heritable changes in gene expression and cellular phenotype that do not involve alterations to the underlying DNA nucleotide sequence.
  • Mechanisms: Covalent addition of methyl groups to the 5-position of cytosine rings (DNA methylation at CpG islands) and post-translational histone modifications (acetylation, methylation).
  • These epigenetic chromatin states are preserved through DNA replication by maintenance methyltransferases (such as DNMT1 in mammals and MET1 in plants) and can be inherited through successive mitotic and meiotic cell divisions.

question: A cross between two true breeding lines, one with dark blue flowers and the other with bright white flowers produces F1 offspring that are light blue. When the F1 progenies are selfed, a 1:2:1 ratio of dark blue to light blue to white flowers is observed. What genetic phenomenon is consistent with these results?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genetics of Incomplete Dominance:
  • Cross: True-breeding dark blue ($BB$) $\times$ True-breeding white ($bb$).
