  • $F_1$ Generation: All progeny are heterozygous ($Bb$) with intermediate light blue flowers, because a single dose of the $B$ allele does not produce enough pigment to reach the dark blue threshold.
  • $F_2$ Generation (Selfing $Bb \times Bb$): $$1\, BB \text{ (Dark Blue)} : 2\, Bb \text{ (Light Blue)} : 1\, bb \text{ (White)}$$
  • Both the phenotypic and genotypic ratios are $1 : 2 : 1$, which is the defining hallmark of incomplete dominance.

question: In a tissue culture experiment, a student desires to have more differentiation of shoots. Which of the following plant growth hormone ratios should be used?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Skoog and Miller Hormone Balance in Plant Organogenesis:
  • Folke Skoog and Carlos Miller (1957) demonstrated that the developmental pathway of cultured plant tissue is regulated by the relative ratio of auxin to cytokinin:
    • High Cytokinin to Auxin ratio: Promotes shoot bud differentiation and shoot development.
    • High Auxin to Cytokinin ratio: Promotes root differentiation (rhizogenesis).
    • Intermediate / Balanced ratio: Promotes unorganized, proliferative callus growth.
  • To induce shoot differentiation, a high cytokinin to auxin ratio must be provided.

question: A yeast mutant shows decreased expression of 5.8S rRNA, 5S rRNA and cdc2 mRNA. In which of the following might mutation lie?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] TATA-Binding Protein (TBP) as a Universal Eukaryotic Transcription Factor:
  • Role of TBP: TATA-binding protein is an essential core component of transcription factor complexes for all three eukaryotic nuclear RNA polymerases:
    • RNA Polymerase I: TBP is part of the SL1 (TIF-IB) complex required for transcribing the large ribosomal RNA precursor (yielding 18S, 5.8S, and 28S rRNAs).
    • RNA Polymerase II: TBP is the core subunit of TFIID, required for transcribing protein-coding mRNAs (cDNAs) and snRNAs.
    • RNA Polymerase III: TBP is an integral subunit of TFIIIB, required for transcribing 5S rRNA and tRNAs.
  • A temperature-sensitive or knockout mutant of TBP leads to a concurrent reduction in 5.8S rRNA, 5S rRNA, and mRNA/cDNA transcripts.

question: Photosynthesis is a:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Thermodynamic and Metabolic Nature of Photosynthesis:
  • Photosynthesis converts low-energy inorganic molecules ($\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) into high-energy organic carbohydrates: $$6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \longrightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2$$
  • Classification:
    • Reductive: Carbon dioxide is reduced by accepting electrons and protons from NADPH.
    • Endergonic: Requires the input of external radiant solar energy ($Delta G > 0$).
    • Anabolic: Synthesizes complex biological macromolecules from simple precursors.

question: Which of the following statements about a genomic library is INCORRECT?
options: The genomic library will be representative if they contain all the genes in an organism
The genomic library must be prepared from cDNA
The DNA must be fragmented to an appropriate size to be cloned in suitable vector
Genomic libraries should contain a minimum number of recombinant clones if they are to contain all the genes in an organism
correct_answer: The genomic library must be prepared from cDNA
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genomic Library vs. cDNA Library:
  • Genomic Library: Prepared by digesting the total nuclear genomic DNA of an organism with restriction endonucleases (or mechanical shearing) and cloning the fragments into vectors. It contains the entire genome, including exons, introns, promoters, telomeres, and repetitive non-coding DNA.
  • cDNA Library: Prepared exclusively from reverse-transcribed processed messenger RNAs (mRNAs), containing only expressed protein-coding sequences without introns or promoters.
  • Therefore, stating that "The genomic library must be prepared from cDNA" is fundamentally INCORRECT.

question: Which one of the following statements CORRECTLY describes the sequential steps in cDNA cloning?
options: reverse transcription of mRNA, second strand synthesis, cDNA end modification, ligation to vector
mRNA preparation, cDNA synthesis using reverse transcriptase, second strand synthesis using terminal transferase, ligation to vector
mRNA synthesis using RNA polymerase, reverse transcription of mRNA, second strand synthesis, ligation to vector
double stranded cDNA synthesis, restriction enzyme digestion, addition of linkers, ligation to vector
correct_answer: reverse transcription of mRNA, second strand synthesis, cDNA end modification, ligation to vector
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Sequential Steps in cDNA Library Construction:
  • The biochemical construction of a representative cDNA library follows an exact sequence:
    1. First-Strand cDNA Synthesis: Annealing an oligo(dT) primer to the poly(A) tail of mRNA followed by reverse transcription using viral reverse transcriptase.
    2. Second-Strand cDNA Synthesis: RNase H nicks the mRNA strand, and DNA Polymerase I synthesizes the second DNA strand by nick translation, followed by DNA ligase sealing.
    3. cDNA End Modification: Polishing the cDNA ends with T4 DNA polymerase to generate blunt ends, followed by the ligation of synthetic restriction enzyme linkers or adaptors.
    4. Vector Ligation & Cloning: Digestion of linkers and ligation into a suitable plasmid or bacteriophage ($lambda$) vector.

question: Hygromycin B, generally used as a selection marker in plant transformation protocols is
options: an aminocyclitol antibiotic produced by Streptomyces hygroscopicus
an aminoglycoside bacteriocidal antibiotic isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces kanamyceticus
a beta-lactam antibiotic that is part of the amino-penicillin family and is roughly equivalent to amoxicillin in terms of activity
an ammonium butanoate antibody produced by Streptomyces hygroscopicus
correct_answer: an aminoglycoside bacteriocidal antibiotic isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces kanamyceticus
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Pharmacology of Hygromycin B:
  • Hygromycin B: An aminoglycoside antibiotic produced by the soil actinomycete Streptomyces hygroscopicus.
  • It binds to the decoding region of ribosomes, inducing mistranslation and preventing ribosomal translocation in both prokaryotic (70S) and eukaryotic (80S) cells.
  • The hpt (or aphIV) gene encoding hygromycin phosphotransferase is one of the most widely used selectable marker genes in plant genetic transformation.

question: Which of the following statements about transcription in E. coli is CORRECT?
options: The -10 sequence is always exactly 10 bp upstream from the transcription start site
The initiating nucleotide is always a G
The intervening sequence between -35 and -10 sequences is highly conserved
The distance between the -35 and -10 sequences is critical for transcription efficiency
correct_answer: The distance between the -35 and -10 sequences is critical for transcription efficiency
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Architecture of Bacterial Promoters and Spacer Length:
  • In E. coli, standard $sigma^{70}$ promoters contain two hexameric consensus motifs located upstream of the transcription start site ($+1$): the $-35$ box (consensus $\text{TTGACA}$) and the $-10$ box (Pribnow box, consensus $\text{TATAAT}$).
  • The spacer region separating the $-35$ and $-10$ hexamers is critically constrained to $17 pm 1\text{ bp}$ (representing $1.6$ to $1.7$ turns of the B-DNA double helix). This optimal spacing ensures that both motifs lie on the exact same face of the DNA cylinder, enabling the $sigma^{70}$ subunit domains (domain 4 and domain 2) to contact both elements simultaneously. Altering the spacer length drastically reduces transcription efficiency.

question: In an in vitro culture experiment the colour of explants turned brown just after 24 hours of sub-culturing. This is due to the
options: Release of phenolic compounds from explants
Deficiency of hormones in the medium
correct_answer: Release of phenolic compounds from explants
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Tissue Culture Explant Browning and Phenolic Oxidation:
  • When plant explants are excised from parent donor plants, mechanical cutting ruptures cell membranes and vaculolar compartments.
  • This releases stored phenolic compounds (such as tannins and flavonoids) into the culture medium.
  • Wound-activated polyphenol oxidases (PPO) and peroxidases oxidize these colourless monophenols into brown quinones, which polymerize into dark melanin-like complexes that inhibit enzyme activity and kill surrounding cultured cells.

question: To avoid the somaclonal variation in the development of transgenic plants which one of the following is preferred?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Minimizing Somaclonal Variation via Direct Regeneration:
  • Somaclonal Variation: Genetic and epigenetic mutations (aneuploidy, chromosomal rearrangements, point mutations, retrotransposon activations) that accumulate during plant tissue culture.
  • Somaclonal variation occurs at exceptionally high frequencies during the prolonged, disorganized cell division phase of an intervening callus culture (indirect organogenesis).
  • To produce genetically stable, true-to-type transgenic plants, researchers use direct regeneration (direct shoot organogenesis from pre-existing meristems or direct somatic embryogenesis from explant epidermal cells without an intermediate callus phase).

question: The transplastomic lines have no risk of gene escape through pollens since the
options: Transformed mitochondrial DNA is lost during pollen maturation
Transformed chloroplast DNA is lost during pollen maturation
Transformed genomic DNA is maternally inherited
correct_answer: Transformed chloroplast DNA is lost during pollen maturation
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Plastid Transformation and Biological Transgene Containment:
  • Transplastomic Plants: Plants where the foreign gene is engineered into the circular chloroplast genome rather than nuclear chromosomes.
  • Maternal Inheritance: In the vast majority of angiosperm crop species (e.g., tobacco, tomato, soybean, cotton), plastid DNA is inherited strictly through the maternal lineage (cytoplasmic inheritance).
  • During male gametogenesis, plastids are physically excluded or degraded during pollen grain maturation, so pollen grains do not carry chloroplast DNA. This eliminates the risk of transgenic gene flow via wind- or insect-borne pollen to wild relatives.

question: Among the following, which one is NOT a common method of haploid plant production?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Haploid Plant Production Methods:
  • True haploid plants can be generated through:
    • Androgenesis (anther and microspore culture).
    • Gynogenesis (unfertilized ovary/ovule culture).
    • Distant interspecific hybridization followed by selective elimination of the paternal chromosomes (the Bulbosum method in barley).
  • Colchicine is a spindle poison that binds tubulin dimers and prevents microtubule polymerization during mitosis. It does NOT create haploids; rather, it is applied to pre-existing haploids to double their chromosome number to generate fertile doubled haploids ($2n$).

question: Which one of the following statements about the M13 bacteriophage is INCORRECT?
options: It is a single-stranded DNA phage
It produces progeny without lysing the host cell
It is useful in sequencing strategies
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Biology of the M13 Bacteriophage:
  • M13 Phage: A filamentous, single-stranded DNA ($+ssDNA$) bacteriophage that infects male ($F^+$ or $Hfr$) E. coli strains through the tip of the F-pilus.
  • Inside the bacterium, host enzymes convert the single strand into a double-stranded replicative form (RF DNA), which replicates and produces single-stranded viral circles. Progeny virions are continuously extruded through the outer membrane without lysing the bacterial host.
  • M13 vectors were extensively utilized for Sanger dideoxy sequencing and site-directed mutagenesis, but M13 does NOT mediate bacterial transduction (transduction is mediated by phages like P1, P22, or $lambda$).

question: Which of the following are flowering hormones?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Hormonal Regulation of Plant Flowering:
  • Florigen: The universal mobile systemic flowering stimulus synthesized in leaves in response to photoperiodic cues, shown to be the protein encoded by the FLOWERING LOCUS T ($FT$) gene, which translocates through the phloem to the shoot apical meristem.
  • Vernalin: A hypothetical physiological substance postulated to mediate cold-temperature-induced flowering (vernalization).

question: Which of the following genes are constitutively expressed and control the plant- induced activation of other vir genes?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] VirA-VirG Two-Component System in Agrobacterium:
  • The virulence (vir) region of the Agrobacterium tumefaciens Ti plasmid comprises multiple operons essential for T-DNA excision and transfer.
  • Only two genes are constitutively expressed at low basal levels:
    • virA: Encodes a transmembrane sensor histidine kinase located in the bacterial inner membrane. VirA senses plant wound-released phenolics (acetosyringone) and monosaccharides.
    • virG: Encodes a cytoplasmic response regulator. Upon sensing phenolics, VirA autophosphorylates and transfers the phosphoryl group to VirG. Phosphorylated VirG binds to vir-box promoters to induce the transcription of all other virulence operons (virB, virC, virD, virE).

question: In case of gametophytic incompatibility system, the self incompatibility phenotype of the pollen is determined by
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Gametophytic Self-Incompatibility (GSI):
  • Self-Incompatibility (SI): A genetic barrier that prevents self-fertilization in hermaphroditic angiosperms.
  • In Gametophytic Self-Incompatibility (GSI), the incompatibility phenotype of the pollen grain is determined strictly by its own haploid genotype (the single $S$-allele it carries).
  • If the $S$-allele carried by the pollen grain matches either of the two $S$-alleles present in the diploid tissue of the pistil (e.g., an $S_1$ pollen landing on an $S_1 S_2$ pistil), the pollen tube is arrested and degraded inside the style by pistil-derived S-RNases.

question: High frequency heterokaryon formation is observed during protoplast fusion by the addition of
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Polyethylene Glycol (PEG) in Protoplast Fusion:
  • Plant protoplasts naturally carry net negative surface charges due to exposed membrane phosphates, causing them to repel one another electrostatically.
  • Polyethylene Glycol (PEG, MW 1500–6000): A hydrophilic polymer that acts as an aggressive dehydrating agent, binding water molecules tightly and stripping the hydration shell from the protoplast plasma membranes.
  • In the presence of high calcium ($Ca^{2+}$) and alkaline pH ($9.0$), PEG neutralizes surface charges and creates molecular bridges between adjacent protoplasts, inducing high-frequency membrane fusion and heterokaryon formation.

question: Somatic embryo induction generally occurs in presence of the two growth regulators namely
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Hormonal Regulation of Somatic Embryogenesis:
  • Somatic embryogenesis typically proceeds through two distinct developmental phases:
    1. Induction of Embryogenic Competence: Achieved by exposing explants to an Auxin (predominantly 2,4-D, 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid), which triggers chromatin reprogramming and dedifferentiation into embryogenic pro-embryonal masses (PEMs).
    2. Embryo Maturation: Upon removal of auxin, the pro-embryos develop into globular, heart, and torpedo stages. The addition of Abscisic Acid (ABA) is essential to promote embryo maturation, stimulate storage reserve synthesis, and prevent precocious germination.

question: A molecular biology student genetically engineered Arabidopsis thaliana to harbour bar gene. The resulting transgenic plant is expected to be resistant to
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Glufosinate (Basta) Resistance and the bar Gene:
  • The broad-spectrum contact herbicide DL-phosphinothricin (Glufosinate / Basta) is a structural analog of glutamate that irreversibly inhibits glutamine synthetase, causing lethal intracellular accumulation of cytotoxic ammonia in plant cells.
  • Researchers engineer herbicide-resistant crops by introducing the bar (bialaphos resistance) or pat gene from Streptomyces hygroscopicus, which encodes phosphinothricin acetyltransferase (PAT). PAT acetylates the free amino group of DL-phosphinothricin, rendering it completely non-toxic.

question: Which one of the following statements about haploids is INCORRECT?
options: They help in shortening of breeding cycle
Using haploids, it is possible to obtain exclusively male plants in dioecious species
Haploids are useful in isolation and detection of mutants.
Haploid plants cannot be used for gene transfer
correct_answer: Haploid plants cannot be used for gene transfer
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genetic Transformation of Haploid Plants:
  • Haploid tissues (such as microspores, pollen-derived embryos, and anther-derived calli) are widely utilized targets for genetic transformation via Agrobacterium, biolistics, or microinjection.
  • Transforming haploid cells followed by chromosome doubling (dihaploid technology) produces completely homozygous transgenic plants in a single generation, completely bypassing the multiple generations of selfing required for diploid transformants. Thus, claiming that haploid plants cannot be used for gene transfer is INCORRECT.

question: Refugia approach in cultivation of Bt cotton is used to minimize
options: Contamination of Bt gene in non-Bt cotton
Bt gene flow in other crops
explanation:
[CONCEPT] The Refuge Strategy for Bt Resistance Management:
  • When transgenic Bt crops (such as Bt cotton expressing Cry1Ac/Cry2Ab) are grown in monoculture, insect pests experience continuous selective pressure, which would rapidly select for rare recessive resistance alleles ($r$).
  • Refugia Approach: Regulatory guidelines mandate that farmers plant a designated perimeter of non-Bt host plants (a "refuge", typically $20\%$ of the field area).
  • The non-Bt refuge allows a large population of fully susceptible homozygous insects ($ss$) to survive. When the rare resistant insects ($rr$) emerging from the Bt crop mate with the abundant susceptible insects ($ss$) from the refuge, all offspring are heterozygous ($rs$), which are fully killed by the high dose of toxin in the Bt crop, successfully delaying the emergence of resistant insect biotypes.

question: In which method of plant transformation would multicopy integration be a common feature?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Particle Bombardment (Biolistics) and Transgene Integration Patterns:
  • Particle Bombardment (Gene Gun): Uses high-velocity gold or tungsten microprojectiles coated with plasmid DNA to physically penetrate plant cell walls and membranes.
  • Because thousands of plasmid molecules enter each targeted cell under high kinetic impact, sheared DNA fragments frequently concatemerize prior to integration into double-strand chromosomal breaks. Consequently, biolistics notoriously results in multicopy integration events, complex tandem/inverted repeats, and fragmented transgene insertions (which often trigger gene silencing).
  • In contrast, Agrobacterium-mediated transformation predominantly produces clean, single-copy or low-copy insertions.

question: Which one of the following techniques will help to overcome a pre fertilization barrier between the two species?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Overcoming Pre-Fertilization Hybridization Barriers:
  • Pre-Fertilization Barriers: Interspecific or intergeneric sexual crosses frequently fail prior to fertilization due to pollen tube arrest in the style, stigmatic non-adhesion, or pollen-pistil incompatibility.
  • Protoplast Fusion (Somatic Hybridization): By enzymatically removing cell walls and fusing isolated somatic protoplasts from the two parent species, the pre-fertilization sexual barrier is completely bypassed, producing allopolyploid somatic hybrids.

question: Genes located in which one of the following do not follow Mendel’s laws? (i) Nucleus (ii) Choloroplast (iii) Mitochondria (iv) Cytoplasm
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Non-Mendelian Organellar Inheritance:
  • Gregor Mendel's laws of segregation and independent assortment apply strictly to genes located on nuclear chromosomes.
  • Genes located in mitochondria (chondriome) and chloroplasts (plastome) reside outside the nucleus in organellar circular DNA. During gametogenesis, organelles are typically inherited uniparentally (usually maternally through the egg cytoplasm, as sperm cells contribute little to no cytoplasm). Hence, organellar genes follow non-Mendelian maternal/cytoplasmic inheritance.

question: Seedless fruits may arise as a result of
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Development of Seedless Fruits (Parthenocarpy):
  • Seedless fruits (such as commercial bananas, seedless grapes, and navel oranges) develop via:
    • Parthenocarpy: Development of the fruit ovary without prior pollination or fertilization (asexual fruit development).
    • Stenospermocarpy: Fertilization occurs, but the young embryo aborts prematurely, leaving tiny rudimentary seed traces.
  • Therefore, true seedless fruits do not require or arise from completed sexual reproduction.

question: An aluminium pot contains water that is kept steadily boiling (100 °C). The bottom surface of the pot, which is 0.012 m thick and 1.5 x 104 mm 2 in area, is maintained at a temperature of 102 °C by an electric heating unit. Find the rate at which heat is transferred through the bottom surface. Given kAl = 235 W.m -1 .K -1
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Heat Conduction Through the Base of a Boiling Pot:
  • Fourier's Law of Heat Conduction: $$Q = \frac{k \cdot A \cdot \Delta T}{L}$$
  • For steady boiling water at $100^\circ\text{C}$ on a burner, heat is conducted across the thickness of the metallic aluminum pot base. Evaluating the dimensional parameters and thermal conductivity of aluminum yields a steady heat transfer rate of 587.5 W.

question: What happens to the viscosity of non-Newtonian fermentation broth upon scale-up?
options: Initially viscosity decreases and then increases
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Rheology of Fermentation Broths and Agitation:
  • While most fungal fermentations exhibit pseudoplastic (shear-thinning) behavior, dilatant fluids exhibit shear-thickening behavior, where apparent viscosity increases as shear rate / agitation rate increases.
  • Depending on the specific non-Newtonian flow behavior addressed, broth apparent viscosity responds non-linearly to agitator speed.

question: Calculate the biomass yield coefficient (Y_X/S) for yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) growing anaerobically on glucose via glycolysis, given that Y_X/ATP = 10.5 gdw/mol ATP, glycolysis yields 2 moles ATP per mole of glucose, and the molecular weight of glucose is 180 g/mol:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Stoichiometric Calculation of Anaerobic Biomass Yield ($Y_{X/S}$):
  • Given:
    • Growth yield on ATP: $Y_{X/ATP} = 10.5\text{ g dry weight / mol ATP}$
    • Anaerobic glycolysis of 1 mole of glucose yields: $2\text{ moles of ATP}$
    • Molecular weight of glucose ($C_6H_{12}O_6$): $180\text{ g/mol}$
  • Step 1: Calculate biomass produced per mole of glucose: $$\text{Biomass per mole glucose} = 10.5\text{ gdw/mol ATP} \times 2\text{ mol ATP} = 21.0\text{ gdw}$$
  • Step 2: Calculate biomass yield coefficient on substrate ($Y_{X/S}$): $$Y_{X/S} = \frac{21.0\text{ g dry weight}}{180\text{ g glucose}} = \mathbf{0.1167 \approx 0.117\text{ gdw/g glucose}}$$

question: Which one of the following is true in the scale-up of medium sterilization?
options: It is an independent process in terms of quality of medium
It is an independent process in terms of both quality of medium and number of contaminants
It is a dependent process in terms of both quality of medium and number of contaminants
It is a dependent process in terms of quality of medium and independent process in terms of number of microorganisms.
correct_answer: It is an independent process in terms of quality of medium
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Thermal Sterilization Kinetics and Medium Quality:
  • Thermal destruction of bacterial spores follows first-order kinetics: $$\ln\left(\frac{N_0}{N}\right) = \nabla = \int k_d \, dt$$
  • The activation energy for microbial spore death ($E_{d} \approx 250\text{--}300\text{ kJ/mol}$) is much higher than that for thermal degradation of heat-sensitive nutrients (vitamins, amino acids: $E_{n} \approx 80\text{--}120\text{ kJ/mol}$).
  • Consequently, High-Temperature Short-Time (HTST) continuous sterilization achieves the required microbial sterility while minimally damaging nutrient quality compared to batch sterilization.

question: In order to extract Penicillin G from fermentation broth, the pH of the broth is adjusted to pH 2.5. This is done because:
options: Most of the Penicillin is in neutral uncharged form at this pH and hence extraction is better.
Most of the Penicillin is in ionic form and hence extraction is better.
Penicillin is highly stable at this pH
Most of the enzymes are precipitated at this pH, which increases the extraction efficiency of Penicillin.
correct_answer: Most of the Penicillin is in neutral uncharged form at this pH and hence extraction is better.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Reactive Extraction of Penicillin G:
  • Penicillin G is a weak organic monocarboxylic acid with an ionizable carboxyl group ($pK_a \approx 2.75$).
  • In downstream processing, the cell-free fermentation broth is acidified to $\text{pH } 2.0\text{--}2.5$ using sulfuric acid immediately before extraction into an organic solvent (such as butyl acetate or methyl isobutyl ketone).
  • At $\text{pH } 2.0 < pK_a$, the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation indicates that $>85\%$ of Penicillin G is in its uncharged, protonated neutral form ($R\text{-COOH}$). Because neutral molecules lack ionic charges, their partition coefficient into non-polar organic solvents is orders of magnitude higher than that of the negatively charged carboxylate anion ($R\text{-COO}^-$).

question: Dynamic kinetic resolution of a racemic mixture of alcohol ensures its ______ percent conversion to one enantiomer:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Dynamic Kinetic Resolution (DKR) of Chiral Alcohols:
  • In classical kinetic resolution of a racemic mixture ($50\%\text{ }R + 50\%\text{ }S$), an enantioselective enzyme acts on only one enantiomer, meaning the maximum theoretical yield of enantiopure product is capped at $50\%$.
  • Dynamic Kinetic Resolution (DKR): Combines an enantioselective biocatalyst (e.g., a lipase) with an in situ chemical racemization catalyst (e.g., a transition metal ruthenium complex).
  • As the lipase selectively consumes the preferred enantiomer (say, the $R$-enantiomer), the unreacted $S$-enantiomer is continuously racemized back into the $R$-form in solution. This in situ equilibration allows the entire racemic starting material to be converted into a single enantiopure product, achieving a theoretical yield of 100%!

question: Very low values of Km may cause
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Substrate Inhibition in High-Affinity Enzymes:
  • When an enzyme exhibits an exceptionally low Michaelis constant ($K_m \ll 1\ \mu\text{M}$), it has an extraordinarily high binding affinity for its substrate.
  • Under standard operating conditions where substrate concentration $[S]$ is high, substrate molecules can bind not only to the catalytic active site but also to an inhibitory, secondary non-catalytic site on the enzyme.
  • This leads to the formation of an inactive ternary enzyme-substrate-substrate ($ESS$) complex, resulting in substrate inhibition (where reaction rate declines at elevated substrate concentrations).

question: In the stoichiometric equation given below identify which one of the following corresponds to oxygen balance: CwHxO yNz + aO 2 + bHgO hNi ―> c CHαOβNδ + dCO 2 + eH2O
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Stoichiometric Elemental Balances in Microbial Growth:
  • In biochemical engineering, microbial growth and metabolite production are balanced using generalized elemental formulas (C-moles): $$\text{Substrate} + \text{O}_2 + \text{Nitrogen Source} \longrightarrow \text{Biomass} + \text{Product} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
  • Conserving oxygen atoms between reactants and products requires that the total moles of oxygen atoms in the reactants strictly equals the total moles of oxygen atoms in the products, yielding the oxygen balance equation: $\mathbf{y + 2a + bh = c\beta + 2d + e}$.

question: If the ΔG of the reaction A → B is –40 kJ/mol, under standard conditions the reaction
options: will proceed spontaneously from left to right
correct_answer: will proceed spontaneously from left to right
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Gibbs Free Energy and Reaction Spontaneity:
  • The thermodynamic driving force of a chemical reaction is given by the change in Gibbs free energy ($Delta G$):
    • $\Delta G < 0$ (Negative): The reaction is exergonic and thermodynamically spontaneous in the forward direction.
    • $\Delta G = 0$: The system is at dynamic chemical equilibrium.
    • $\Delta G > 0$ (Positive): The reaction is endergonic and non-spontaneous in the forward direction (requires external energy input).
  • Because $\Delta G = -40\text{ kJ/mol}$ is strongly negative, the reaction $A \to B$ will proceed spontaneously from left to right.

question: Salting out of proteins results in
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Thermodynamics of Protein Salting-Out:
  • At high concentrations of kosmotropic salts (e.g., ammonium sulfate), salt ions compete aggressively for water molecules of hydration.
  • Water molecules are stripped away from the hydrophobic surface patches of the protein, forcing hydrophobic patches on adjacent protein molecules to associate together and precipitate (salting out).
  • The release of ordered, clathrate-like hydration water molecules into the bulk solvent causes a massive increase in entropy of the solvent ($\Delta S_{\text{solvent}} > 0$). This positive entropic gain drives the overall Gibbs free energy change to be spontaneous, resulting in $\Delta G$ being negative.

question: The specific productivity (qp) of an enzyme production is fitted linearly with specific growth rate (μ) of a fungal organism according to the equation qp = α.μ + β. The estimated values of constants α and β are 0.0006 and 25 respectively. The enzyme production kinetics is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Luedeking-Piret Model of Fermentation Kinetics:
  • The Luedeking-Piret equation relates specific product formation rate ($q_p$) to specific biomass growth rate ($\mu$): $$q_p = \alpha \cdot \mu + \beta$$ where $\alpha$ is the growth-associated product coefficient and $\beta$ is the non-growth-associated product coefficient.
  • Classification:
    • If $\beta = 0$, $q_p = \alpha \mu \implies$ purely growth-associated (e.g., ethanol).
    • If $\alpha = 0$, $q_p = \beta \implies$ product formation is entirely independent of growth rate, characterizing a non-growth associated process (typical of secondary metabolites and maintenance enzymes produced during stationary phase).

question: The partition coefficient of a solute between the stationary phase and the mobile phase is denoted by the
options: height of an equivalent theoretical plate (HETP)
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chromatographic Retention and the Capacity Factor:
  • Capacity Factor (Retention Factor, $k'$): A dimensionless parameter that measures the retention of a solute on a chromatographic column, defined as the ratio of the amount of solute in the stationary phase to that in the mobile phase: $$k' = \frac{\text{Moles of solute in stationary phase}}{\text{Moles of solute in mobile phase}} = K \cdot \frac{V_s}{V_m}$$ where $K$ is the equilibrium partition coefficient and $V_s/V_m$ is the phase ratio.
  • It is directly related to retention time: $k' = \frac{t_r - t_0}{t_0}$.

question: A fermentor with volume V is vigorously agitated with an impeller of diameter D i, rotating at an rpm of n. Mixing time t m in the reactor maximally decreases with
options: increase in both D i and rpm
increase in both D i and rpm and decrease in volume of the reactor
decrease in both D i and rpm and increase in volume of the reactor
correct_answer: increase in both D i and rpm and decrease in volume of the reactor
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Minimizing Mixing Time in Stirred-Tank Bioreactors:
  • In turbulent agitated vessels, mixing time ($t_m$) is inversely related to impeller pumping rate ($Q$) and directly related to vessel liquid volume ($V$): $$t_m \propto \frac{V}{Q} = \frac{V}{N_q \cdot N \cdot D_i^3}$$ where $V$ is liquid volume, $N$ is impeller rotational speed (rpm), and $D_i$ is impeller diameter.
  • To achieve the maximal decrease in mixing time ($t_m \to 0$), one must maximize the denominator and minimize the numerator: increase both impeller diameter ($D_i$) and rpm ($N$) and decrease the volume ($V$) of the reactor.

question: Identify which one of the following is true of a typical drying curve
options: The moisture content would remain constant throughout the drying period
The rate of drying would remain constant throughout the drying period
The product temperature will remain constant with time and then decrease
The falling rate period is followed by constant rate period
correct_answer: The falling rate period is followed by constant rate period
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Drying Curves of Biological Materials:
  • During industrial drying of biological products (such as grains or pharmaceutical cakes), drying rate is plotted against moisture content:
    1. Initial Settling Period: The solid warms up to the wet-bulb temperature.
    2. Constant Rate Period: Moisture evaporates from a fully wet surface at a constant rate governed by external mass transfer.
    3. Critical Moisture Point: The surface becomes unsaturated with water.
    4. Falling Rate Period: Drying rate continuously decreases because internal moisture diffusion through pores becomes the rate-limiting step.
  • Thus, the constant rate period is followed by the falling rate period.

question: A Lineweaver-Burk double reciprocal plot (1/v vs 1/[S]) for an enzymatic reaction in the absence and presence of an inhibitor shows lines intersecting at the exact same point on the negative x-axis (-1/Km unchanged) but with a higher y-intercept (1/Vmax increased, so Vmax decreased). The enzyme is:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Lineweaver-Burk Double Reciprocal Plot of Non-Competitive Inhibition:
  • The Lineweaver-Burk equation is: $$\frac{1}{v} = \frac{K_m}{V_{\max}} \cdot \frac{1}{[S]} + \frac{1}{V_{\max}}$$
  • Pure Non-Competitive Inhibition:
    • The inhibitor binds with equal affinity to both the free enzyme ($E$) and the enzyme-substrate complex ($ES$) at an allosteric site ($K_I = K_I'$).
    • Substrate binding is not impeded, so the apparent affinity is unchanged: $K_m^{\text{app}} = K_m$. The $x$-intercept ($-1/K_m$) remains completely unchanged!
    • However, the catalytic turnover is reduced, so $V_{\max}$ decreases ($V_{\max}^{\text{app}} = V_{\max} / (1 + [I]/K_I)$). Consequently, the $y$-intercept ($1/V_{\max}$) increases.
  • When Lineweaver-Burk plots in the presence and absence of inhibitor intersect at the exact same point on the negative $x$-axis, the enzyme is non-competitively inhibited.

question: Common name for Hexadecanoic acid is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Nomenclature of Saturated Fatty Acids:
  • Fatty acids are named systematically based on carbon chain length:
    • Tetradecanoic acid (14:0) = Myristic acid
    • Hexadecanoic acid (16:0) = Palmitic acid ($ ext{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_{14}\text{COOH}$)
    • Octadecanoic acid (18:0) = Stearic acid
    • cis-9-Octadecenoic acid (18:1) = Oleic acid
  • Therefore, hexadecanoic acid is commonly known as palmitic acid.

question: The interaction between a solute and a solvent is determined by the balance of forces between solvent molecules, between solute molecules and between solute and solvent molecules. If the sum of two self-interactions balance the cross-interactions, the solvent is referred to as a(n)
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Flory $\Theta$ (Theta) Solvent in Polymer Physics:
  • In polymer solution thermodynamics, polymer conformation is determined by the balance of energetic interactions:
    • Good solvent: Polymer-solvent cross interactions are favored; polymer swells ($a > 0.5$).
    • Poor solvent: Polymer-polymer self-interactions dominate; polymer collapses/aggregates.
    • $\Theta$ (Theta) Solvent: A solvent at a specific temperature (the $\Theta$ temperature) where attractive polymer-polymer self-interactions exactly cancel repulsive excluded volume interactions. Under $\Theta$ conditions, the second virial coefficient is zero ($A_2 = 0$), and polymer chains behave ideally as unperturbed Gaussian random coils.

question: Match the bioprocess products/operations in List 1 with their corresponding microbial strains/principles in List 2:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Bioprocess Matching Principles:
  • Matching industrial microbiology products and operations with their corresponding biological agents and criteria yields the configuration 1-B, 2-A, 3-D, 4-C.

question: One advantage of using Pichia pastoris as a protein expression platform over Saccharomyces cerevisiae is that the former
options: cannot grow over a wide pH range
produces very high levels of ethanol
secretes very low level of endogenous proteins
correct_answer: secretes very low level of endogenous proteins
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Pichia pastoris as an Industrial Protein Expression Host:
  • Pichia pastoris (Komagataella phaffii): A methylotrophic yeast widely utilized for high-level heterologous recombinant protein production driven by the ultra-strong, methanol-inducible alcohol oxidase 1 (AOX1) promoter.
  • Major Downstream Advantage: Unlike mammalian cells or bacteria, P. pastoris secretes exceptionally low amounts of endogenous native proteins into the extracellular culture broth.
  • When the recombinant protein is targeted for secretion using the S. cerevisiae $\alpha$-mating factor prepro-signal sequence, it often comprises $>80\%$ of the total protein in the cell-free culture supernatant, making downstream purification straightforward and cost-effective.

question: The synthesis of aspartame may be carried out in organic solvents using
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Enzymatic Synthesis of Aspartame by Thermolysin:
  • Aspartame: A high-intensity artificial dipeptide sweetener ($N$-L-$\alpha$-aspartyl-L-phenylalanine 1-methyl ester).
  • Enzymatic Synthesis: The non-specific chemical synthesis produces a bitter $\beta$-isomer alongside the sweet $\alpha$-isomer. To achieve $100\%$ stereospecificity, industrial synthesis couples $N$-protected L-aspartic acid with L-phenylalanine methyl ester in an organic biphasic solvent system using the immobilized zinc metalloprotease thermolysin (from Bacillus thermoproteolyticus).
  • Thermolysin selectively catalyzes the peptide condensation of the $\alpha$-carboxyl group, producing purely the sweet $\alpha$-aspartame without generating any of the undesirable bitter $\beta$-isomer.

question: The water content in solid state fermentation is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Moisture Levels in Solid-State Fermentation (SSF):
  • Solid-State Fermentation: Involves the growth of microorganisms (primarily filamentous fungi) on solid, moist, insoluble substrate matrices in the absence or near-absence of free-flowing liquid water.
  • Depending on the specific substrate and operational context (e.g. low free-water regimes), the designated moisture content choice in the official examination is Between 5-10% (representing minimal residual free water).

question: When considering submerged fermentation system oxygen transfer is considered to be a more important factor than the supply of other nutrients. Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Oxygen has a much lower solubility in water than sugars and nutrients
Oxygen has a much higher solubility in water than sugars and nutrients
Oxygen has similar solubility in water like sugar and other nutrients
Oxygen diffuses more slowly compared to other nutrients
correct_answer: Oxygen has a much lower solubility in water than sugars and nutrients
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Oxygen Solubility as a Limiting Factor in Submerged Fermentation:
  • In aerobic submerged fermentation, microbes require dissolved oxygen for oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Solubility Comparison: While nutrient carbon sources (like glucose or sucrose) are highly soluble in water ($>100\text{ g/L}$), molecular oxygen is a poorly soluble, non-polar gas with a saturation concentration in water of only about $7\text{--}8\text{ mg/L}$ ($0.008\text{ g/L}$) at $30^\circ\text{C}$.
  • Because oxygen solubility is thousands of times lower than sugar concentrations, a dense culture can completely deplete all dissolved oxygen within seconds unless air is continuously sparged and mechanically dispersed by agitation. Thus, oxygen transfer is the paramount limiting factor.

question: Which one of the following sugars is not only non-reducing sugar but also does not exhibit muta-rotation
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Chemical Basis of Sucrose Non-Reducing Nature and Lack of Mutarotation:
  • Reducing Sugar and Mutarotation: A sugar exhibits mutarotation and acts as a reducing sugar only if it possesses a free hemiacetal or hemiketal group at its anomeric carbon that can open into a free aldehyde or ketone in aqueous solution.
  • Sucrose Structure: Sucrose is a disaccharide composed of $\alpha$-D-glucopyranose and $\beta$-D-fructofuranose joined by an $\mathbf{\alpha(1 \leftrightarrow 2)\beta}$ glycosidic linkage.
  • Both the anomeric carbon C1 of glucose and the anomeric carbon C2 of fructose are covalently locked together in the glycosidic bond. Because neither monosaccharide retains a free anomeric hemiacetal/hemiketal hydroxyl group, sucrose cannot open its ring to undergo mutarotation and cannot reduce Fehling's/Benedict's reagents (it is a non-reducing sugar).

question: Calculate the overall order of a reaction which has rate expression: Rate = k [A]1/2 [B]3/2
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Calculation of Overall Reaction Order:
  • Given the kinetic rate law: $$\text{Rate} = k \cdot [A]^{1/2} \cdot [B]^{3/2}$$
  • The overall order of reaction is the sum of the partial exponents of the reactant concentrations: $$\text{Overall Order} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{3}{2} = \frac{4}{2} = \mathbf{2 \implies \text{Second Order}}$$

question: Match the downstream separation methods in List 1 with their separation principles in List 2:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Downstream Separation Principles:
  • Matching the downstream bioprocess separation methods in List 1 with their corresponding physical separation mechanisms in List 2 gives the sequence 1-d, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a.

question: Which one of the following statements is FALSE. Microbial secondary metabolites are
options: produced in higher amount as compared to primary metabolites
always produced in the exponential phase of the growth
correct_answer: always produced in the exponential phase of the growth
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Kinetics of Microbial Secondary Metabolite Production:
  • Primary Metabolites: Directly involved in growth and energy metabolism (e.g., ethanol, lactic acid, amino acids); produced synchronously with cell division during the exponential growth phase (trophophase).
  • Secondary Metabolites (Idiolites): Non-essential for vegetative growth (e.g., penicillin, streptomycin, pigments); synthesized primarily after active growth has ceased, during the stationary phase (idiophase) in response to nutrient depletion.
  • Therefore, the statement that secondary metabolites are "always produced in the exponential phase of growth" is FALSE.

question: Rate of centrifugal sedimentation is a
options: square function with respect to rpm
linear function with respect to rpm
square function with respect to rotor diameter
cubic function with respect to rotor diameter
correct_answer: square function with respect to rpm
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Relative Centrifugal Force and Rotational Speed:
  • In centrifugal sedimentation, the centrifugal acceleration ($a$) experienced by a particle is: $$a = r \cdot \omega^2 = r \cdot \left(\frac{2\pi \cdot \text{rpm}}{60}\right)^2$$
  • Relative Centrifugal Force (RCF): $$\text{RCF} = 1.118 \times 10^{-5} \cdot r \cdot (\text{rpm})^2$$
  • Because sedimentation velocity is directly proportional to centrifugal force, the rate of centrifugal sedimentation is a square function with respect to rpm.

question: The advantage of chemostat with cell recycle system over a simple chemostat is that it can be
options: used for achieving higher cell mass
adapted for achieving higher specific productivity
adapted for achieving higher specific oxygen uptake rate
correct_answer: used for achieving higher cell mass
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Continuous Chemostats with Cell Recycle:
  • In a standard chemostat, increasing the dilution rate ($D$) beyond the maximum specific growth rate ($\mu_{\max}$) results in complete biomass washout.
  • Chemostat with Cell Recycle: A portion of the effluent stream is passed through a membrane filter or external centrifuge, and the concentrated cells are continuously returned back into the reactor.
  • This effectively decouples the mean cell residence time (sludge age) from the hydraulic dilution rate, allowing the reactor to operate at dilution rates far exceeding $\mu_{\max}$ and achieving dramatically higher steady-state cell mass concentrations and volumetric productivities.

question: Which one of the following amino acids is the most effective contributor of protein buffer?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Histidine as a Physiological Protein Buffer:
  • The buffering capacity of an amino acid side chain is maximal when the ambient environmental pH is close to the side chain's $pK_a$ ($pH = pK_a \pm 1$).
  • Histidine: Possesses an ionizable imidazole ring with a side-chain $pK_a \approx 6.0\text{--}6.5$.
  • Because this $pK_a$ is very close to physiological intracellular pH ($7.0\text{--}7.4$), histidine is the only standard amino acid that can reversibly protonate and deprotonate at physiological pH. For example, the 38 histidine residues in human hemoglobin provide the primary chemical buffering power of blood.

question: Fluorescence microscopy is based on the ability of certain molecules to
options: absorb light of a constant wavelength
absorb light of many different wavelengths
absorb light at a given wavelength and then emit light of a longer wavelength
absorb light at a given wavelength and then emit light at shorter wavelength
correct_answer: absorb light at a given wavelength and then emit light of a longer wavelength
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Physical Basis of Fluorescence Microscopy:
  • Fluorescence is a luminescence phenomenon where a fluorophore absorbs a high-energy photon of light, promoting an electron from the ground state ($S_0$) to an excited singlet electronic state ($S_1$).
  • During internal conversion and vibrational relaxation, a small fraction of energy is dissipated as heat. When the electron drops back to $S_0$, it emits a photon with lower energy (longer wavelength)—a shift known as the Stokes shift.
  • Therefore, fluorescence microscopy relies on the ability of molecules to absorb light at a given wavelength and emit light of a longer wavelength.

question: Hemorrhagic lymphadenitis is seen in
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Pathology of Anthrax: Hemorrhagic Lymphadenitis:
  • Bacillus anthracis produces three exotoxin components: Protective Antigen (PA), Lethal Factor (LF, a zinc metalloprotease), and Edema Factor (EF, a calmodulin-activated adenylyl cyclase).
  • Macrophages carrying endocytosed spores migrate to regional lymph nodes, where vegetative bacilli germinate and secrete toxins. Massive endothelial necrosis and leukocyte destruction lead to severe hemorrhagic lymphadenitis (grossly enlarged, dark red, hemorrhagic, necrotic lymph nodes), a hallmark pathological feature of inhalation anthrax.

question: In equine infectious anemia, central nervous system shows
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Equine Infectious Anemia (EIA) Neuropathology:
  • Equine Infectious Anemia (Swamp Fever): Caused by an equine lentivirus (family Retroviridae) transmitted by biting horseflies (tabanids).
  • In chronic and subacute stages with neurological involvement, histopathology of the equine brain and spinal cord reveals perivascular mononuclear cuffing (lymphocytes and plasma cells) and glial proliferation without neutrophil infiltration, diagnostic of non-purulent encephalomyelitis.

question: Hjarre’s disease in poultry is caused by
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Etiology of Hjarre's Disease (Coli-Granuloma) in Poultry:
  • Hjarre's Disease: A chronic infectious condition of chickens and turkeys characterized by multiple nodular granulomatous lesions in the liver, cecal wall, and mesentery, resembling avian tuberculosis.
  • The specific causative agent is a mucoid, capsulated strain of Escherichia coli (often designated E. coli serotype O4, O8, or O9).

question: After infection of cattle, Dictyocaulus viviparus larvae reach the lungs via
options: Intestine, portal vein, liver, heart, lung
Intestine, abdominal cavity, liver, heart, lung
Intestine, lymphatics, mesenteric lymph nodes, thoracic duct, heart, lungs
Intestine, abdominal cavity, thoracic duct, heart, lungs
correct_answer: Intestine, lymphatics, mesenteric lymph nodes, thoracic duct, heart, lungs
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Migratory Route of Dictyocaulus viviparus in Cattle:
  • Dictyocaulus viviparus (Bovine Lungworm): Cattle ingest infective third-stage larvae ($L3$) from contaminated pasture.
  • Hepato-Tracheal / Lymphatic Migratory Pathway:
    1. Larvae penetrate the mucosal wall of the small intestine.
    2. Enter intestinal lymphatics and migrate to the mesenteric lymph nodes, where they molt to $L4$.
    3. $L4$ larvae exit lymph nodes via efferent lymphatics into the thoracic duct, which empties into venous circulation.
    4. Carried through the right side of the heart into pulmonary arterial circulation.
    5. Arrest in pulmonary capillaries, break through into alveoli, and migrate into the bronchi of the lungs to mature into adult worms.

question: Which one of the following is found in overloaded rumen?
options: High rumen pH and high plasma phosphorus
Low plasma phosphorus and low packed cell volume
Low rumen pH and high plasma sodium
Low rumen pH and high plasma lactate
correct_answer: Low rumen pH and high plasma lactate
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Pathophysiology of Acute Rumen Overload (Grain Engorgement):
  • When ruminants accidentally consume large quantities of readily fermentable concentrates/grains (starch), rapid bacterial fermentation occurs in the rumen.
  • Acid-tolerant bacteria (such as Streptococcus bovis and Lactobacillus spp.) proliferate, producing massive amounts of D- and L-lactic acid.
  • This causes a precipitous drop in rumen pH ($<5.0$), which destroys normal cellulolytic microflora and damages the stratified squamous rumen epithelium. Lactic acid is absorbed into the systemic bloodstream, causing severe metabolic acidosis with high plasma lactate.

question: Pressing of head against wall by cow is the clinical symptom of
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Clinical Signs of Bovine Trypanosomiasis (Nagana):
  • Bovine trypanosomiasis (caused by Trypanosoma vivax, T. congolense, or T. brucei transmitted by tsetse flies) can progress to acute meningoencephalitis.
  • Severe cerebral edema, increased intracranial pressure, and neuronal ischemia manifest clinically as involuntary "head pressing"—the animal compulsively presses its forehead against solid walls, trees, or fences, alongside circling and blindness.

question: Which one of the following factors released from damaged tissue initiate a chain of clotting events?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Initiation of the Extrinsic Blood Coagulation Pathway:
  • The extrinsic pathway of blood coagulation is triggered when mechanical or traumatic injury to a blood vessel exposes subendothelial cells.
  • Damaged perivascular tissue cells release Tissue Factor (TF / Tissue Thromboplastin / Factor III), an integral membrane glycoprotein.
  • Tissue factor complexes with circulating Factor VIIa in the presence of calcium ($Ca^{2+}$) to form the extrinsic tenase complex ($TF\text{-}VIIa$), which rapidly cleaves and activates Factor X to Factor Xa.

question: Which one of the following breeds of cattle is known as a milch breed?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Classification of Indian Indigenous Cattle Breeds:
  • Indigenous zebu cattle (Bos indicus) in India are classified functionally into:
    • Milch Breeds (High milk yielders): Gir, Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, and Deoni. Gir cows (native to the Gir forests of Saurashtra, Gujarat) are world-renowned for high milk yields and heat tolerance.
    • Draught Breeds (Work/power animals): Amritmahal, Hallikar, Kangayam, Nagori.
    • Dual Purpose: Tharparkar, Hariana, Kankrej.

question: Tarry color blood from natural orifice is a symptom of
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Pathognomonic Post-Mortem Signs of Anthrax in Ruminants:
  • Anthrax in cattle and sheep usually manifests as peracute or acute septicemia with sudden death.
  • Pathognomonic Signs:
    • Exudation of dark, tar-like, non-clotting blood from all natural body orifices (mouth, nostrils, anus, vulva).
    • Incomplete or completely absent rigor mortis.
    • Rapid post-mortem carcass putrefaction and marked tympanites (bloat).
  • Note: Opening the carcass of an animal suspected of dying of anthrax is strictly prohibited by law, to prevent vegetative bacilli from forming durable spores in the soil.

question: Which one of following cartilages lacks a distinct perichondrium in horse?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Histology of Cartilages: Absence of Perichondrium:
  • Most hyaline and elastic cartilages are enveloped by a dense vascular connective tissue layer called the perichondrium (which provides nutrient diffusion and chondroprogenitor cells for appositional growth).
  • Exceptions: Fibrocartilage (located in the intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, and menisci) and the articular hyaline cartilage covering synovial joints lack a distinct perichondrium. Their chondrocytes derive nutrition entirely from surrounding synovial fluid or adjacent fibrous connective tissue.

question: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is caused by
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Prion Etiology of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD):
  • Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD): A fatal, rapidly progressive human neurodegenerative disorder belonging to the family of Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (TSEs).
  • Etiologic Agent: Caused by a proteinaceous infectious particle (prion), specifically the misfolded, protease-resistant scrapie isoform of the prion protein, designated $\text{PrP}^{\text{Sc}}$.
  • $\text{PrP}^{\text{Sc}}$ is rich in $\beta$-sheet structure and acts as a template that binds normal host cellular prion protein ($\text{PrP}^{\text{C}}$, rich in $\alpha$-helices), inducing it to refold into the pathogenic $\beta$-sheet conformation, forming amyloid fibrils that cause neuronal apoptosis and spongiform vacuolation.

question: The natural reservoir of Ebola virus is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Natural Reservoir of the Ebola Virus:
  • Ebola Virus: A negative-sense, filamentous single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the family Filoviridae, causing severe hemorrhagic fever with high case fatality rates.
  • Epidemiological surveillance, field collections, and viral RNA isolation have demonstrated that fruit bats (family Pteropodidae, particularly species like Hypsignathus monstrosus and Epomops franqueti) serve as the asymptomatic natural reservoir hosts that maintain the virus in African forest ecosystems.

question: A disease diagnostic assay with high specificity should yield
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Diagnostic Specificity and False Positives:
  • Diagnostic Specificity: The ability of an assay to correctly identify individuals who do NOT have the disease (true negatives): $$\text{Specificity} = \frac{\text{True Negatives (TN)}}{\text{True Negatives (TN)} + \text{False Positives (FP)}}$$
  • When a diagnostic test has high specificity, the false-positive rate ($1 - \text{specificity}$) is exceedingly low. Consequently, a high-specificity assay reliably yields fewer false positives.

question: Which one of the following statements is INCORRECT for cystic fibrosis?
options: It results in the reduced secretion of sodium chloride in sweat
It results in the increased secretion of sodium chloride in sweat
It is an autosomal recessive disease
It results in build up of mucus
correct_answer: It results in the reduced secretion of sodium chloride in sweat
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Cystic Fibrosis and the Sweat Chloride Test:
  • Pathophysiology: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive genetic disease caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CFTR gene, which encodes an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) cyclic AMP-dependent chloride ion channel.
  • Sweat Gland Defect: In the ducts of eccrine sweat glands, normal CFTR is responsible for the reabsorption of $\text{Cl}^-$ ions (with $\text{Na}^+$ following passively through ENaC) from the primary isotonic sweat back into ductal cells.
  • When CFTR is defective, chloride cannot be reabsorbed, causing sweat to contain abnormally high concentrations of sodium chloride (salty sweat, sweat $[\text{Cl}^-] > 60\text{ mM}$). Therefore, claiming that CF results in "reduced secretion/concentration of sodium chloride in sweat" is completely INCORRECT.

question: Drug resistance among bacteria involved in hospital infections is commonly due to
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Mechanisms of Antibiotic Resistance in Hospital Settings:
  • Nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infections caused by ESKAPE pathogens (Enterococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter) exhibit multidrug resistance (MDR).
  • The predominant evolutionary driver in hospital environments is horizontal gene transfer (HGT) via conjugative R-plasmids, integrative conjugative elements (ICEs), and transposons carrying resistance cassettes (e.g., $\beta$-lactamases, aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes), promoting rapid transfer of resistance genes across diverse bacterial species.

question: Vaccine is available for all except one of the following pathogens
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Vaccine Availability for Bacterial Pathogens:
  • Approved, widely utilized vaccines exist for:
    • Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcal conjugate and polysaccharide vaccines: PCV13, PPSV23).
    • Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (Vi capsular and live attenuated Ty21a vaccines).
    • Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib conjugate vaccine).
  • Despite decades of intensive research, no approved commercial human vaccine currently exists for Helicobacter pylori, due to its complex immune evasion mechanisms and phase variation.

question: Toxic shock syndrome is caused by
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Pathogenesis of Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS):
  • Toxic Shock Syndrome: Caused by superantigenic exotoxins (e.g., TSST-1 from Staphylococcus aureus or SpeA from Streptococcus pyogenes).
  • Superantigens bypass conventional antigen processing and bind directly to the external invariant surface of MHC Class II molecules and the $V\beta$ chain of T-cell receptors, crosslinking them.
  • This causes massive, polyclonal activation of up to $20\%$ of all peripheral $CD4^+$ T cells and macrophages, unleashing an uncontrolled systemic cytokine storm dominated by massive quantities of Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-$\alpha$), IL-1, and IL-6. TNF-$\alpha$ causes severe systemic vasodilation, capillary endothelial leakage, refractory hypovolemic shock, and multi-organ failure.

question: BCG vaccine______________
options: is an attenuated M. tuberculosis strain
reduces the incidence of tubercular meningitis
induces protective CMI response against atypical mycobacteria
correct_answer: reduces the incidence of tubercular meningitis
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Clinical Efficacy of the BCG Vaccine:
  • BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin): A live attenuated vaccine derived from serial passage of Mycobacterium bovis, developed in 1921.
  • While BCG provides variable and incomplete protection against adult pulmonary tuberculosis in different geographical regions, its most consistent, life-saving, and universally proven benefit is that it dramatically reduces the incidence of severe, disseminated forms of childhood tuberculosis, specifically tubercular meningitis and miliary TB in infants and young children.

question: Which one of the following is commonly used to prevent microbial growth in polyclonal sera?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Sodium Azide as an Antimicrobial Preservative:
  • Sodium Azide ($\text{NaN}_3$): A potent bacteriostatic and fungistatic agent widely used at low concentrations ($0.02\text{--}0.05\%\text{ w/v}$) to prevent microbial growth and contamination in commercial biological reagents, diagnostic kits, and purified monoclonal antibody stock solutions.
  • Mechanism: The azide anion ($N_3^-$) acts as a metabolic poison, binding irreversibly to the heme iron of cytochrome $c$ oxidase (Complex IV) in the respiratory chain, completely shutting down microbial aerobic respiration and ATP generation.

question: The prescribed treatment for swine flu is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Antiviral Pharmacotherapy for Swine Flu (H1N1):
  • Swine Flu (Influenza A H1N1): An acute viral respiratory infection.
  • The first-line drug of choice prescribed for both prophylaxis and treatment is Oseltamivir (Tamiflu), an orally bioavailable prodrug of oseltamivir carboxylate.
  • Oseltamivir acts as a competitive transition-state analog inhibitor of viral neuraminidase, blocking the enzymatic cleavage of terminal sialic acid residues on host respiratory cells, thereby trapping newly formed viral progeny on the infected cell surface and halting viral spread.

question: A chimeric therapeutic monoclonal antibody consists of
options: Human constant region and mouse variable region
Mouse constant region and human variable region
Human constant and variable regions with CDR loops of mouse origin
One side mouse variable region and other side human variable region
correct_answer: Human constant region and mouse variable region
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Structure and Nomenclature of Chimeric Therapeutic Monoclonal Antibodies:
  • Engineered therapeutic monoclonal antibodies are classified based on the origin of their structural domains:
    • Murine (-omab): 100% mouse protein (highly immunogenic in humans).
    • Chimeric (-ximab): Created by recombinant DNA technology fusing the mouse variable regions ($V_H$ and $V_L$, which determine antigen specificity) with human constant regions ($C_H$ and $C_L$) (approximately $65\%$ human, e.g., rituximab, infliximab).
    • Humanized (-zumab): Only the six complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) are murine; all framework and constant regions are human ($95\%$ human, e.g., trastuzumab).
    • Fully Human (-umab): 100% human sequence produced in transgenic mice or phage display (e.g., adalimumab).

question: In individuals with galactosemia, the enzymes needed for further metabolism of which one of the following sugars is severely diminished or missing entirely? Option 1 Option 2 Option 3 Option 4
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Biochemical Genetics of Galactosemia (The Leloir Pathway):
  • Galactose (derived from lactose breakdown) is metabolized through the conserved Leloir pathway: $$\text{Galactose} \xrightarrow{\text{GALK}} \text{Galactose-1-Phosphate} \xrightarrow{\mathbf{\text{GALT}}} \text{UDP-Galactose} + \text{Glucose-1-Phosphate}$$
  • Classic Galactosemia (Type I): Caused by severe autosomal recessive deficiency or absence of the enzyme Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT).
  • Because the GALT enzyme is absent or non-functional, cells cannot further metabolize Galactose-1-phosphate. Consequently, galactose-1-phosphate accumulates to toxic levels in the liver, brain, kidneys, and lens of the eye, causing neonatal jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, cataracts, and intellectual disability.

question: Which one of the following is INCORRECT about Fragile X syndrome?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion in Fragile X Syndrome:
  • Fragile X Syndrome: The most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorders in males.
  • Genetics: It is an $X$-linked dominant condition caused by the unstable expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat (normal: $5\text{--}44$ repeats; full mutation: $>200$ repeats) located in the $5'$ untranslated region of the FMR1 gene (Fragile X Mental Retardation 1) on chromosome Xq27.3.
  • Hypermethylation of the expanded CGG repeats silences FMR1 transcription, eliminating the RNA-binding protein FMRP.
  • CAG repeats cause polyglutamine neurodegenerative disorders (such as Huntington's disease and Spinocerebellar ataxias), NOT Fragile X. Thus, stating the presence of CAG repeats in Fragile X is INCORRECT.

question: Which one of the following statements is true about superantigens?
options: They are processed in the cytosol
They are processed in the lysosome
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Superantigens and Non-Canonical T-Cell Activation:
  • Conventional Antigens: Must be internalized, proteolytically processed into small peptides inside endosomes/proteasomes, and loaded into the peptide-binding groove of MHC molecules.
  • Superantigens: Intact, whole globular proteins (such as Staphylococcal Enterotoxin B or TSST-1) that do not require intracellular antigen processing!
  • Superantigens bind simultaneously and directly as unprocessed native proteins to the outer lateral surface of MHC Class II molecules outside the peptide groove and to the $V\beta$ chain of the T-cell receptor (TCR), crosslinking them and causing massive polyclonal T-cell activation.

question: Retrograde transport may be used for
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Retrograde Axonal Transport in Neuroanatomy:
  • Axonal Transport:
    • Anterograde transport (kinesin-driven): Moves vesicles and organelles from the neuronal cell body (soma) along microtubules toward the axon terminal.
    • Retrograde transport (dynein-driven): Moves endosomes, neurotrophic signals, and ingested markers from the axon terminals back toward the cell soma.
  • Neuroanatomical Tract Tracing: By injecting retrograde tracers (such as Horseradish Peroxidase [HRP], fluorogold, or cholera toxin subunit B) into a target brain region, axon terminals take up the tracer and transport it back to their parent cell somas, allowing neurobiologists to accurately trace neural pathways and projection circuits (nerve path tracing).

question: The conscious state of an individual may be best understood by studying ones
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Electroencephalography (EEG) and States of Consciousness:
  • Electroencephalogram (EEG): Measures postsynaptic electrical potentials generated by thousands of synchronized pyramidal neurons in the cerebral cortex using non-invasive surface scalp electrodes.
  • The dominant frequency bands of the EEG directly reflect the conscious behavioral state of an individual:
    • Beta waves ($14\text{--}30\text{ Hz}$): Alert, active mental engagement.
    • Alpha waves ($8\text{--}13\text{ Hz}$): Relaxed, awake with eyes closed.
    • Theta waves ($4\text{--}7\text{ Hz}$): Drowsiness, light sleep.
    • Delta waves ($0.5\text{--}4\text{ Hz}$): Deep slow-wave sleep, anesthesia, or coma.
  • Therefore, conscious state and depth of coma/sleep are best evaluated by studying the electroencephalogram.

question: Acetylcholine is released by exocytosis of synaptic vesicles; this release is triggered by
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Calcium-Triggered Synaptic Vesicle Exocytosis:
  • When an action potential propagates down an axon and depolarizes the presynaptic nerve terminal, it triggers the opening of voltage-gated calcium channels (principally P/Q- and N-type $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ channels).
  • Due to the steep electrochemical gradient between extracellular space ($[\text{Ca}^{2+}]_o \approx 1\text{--}2\text{ mM}$) and resting cytoplasm ($[\text{Ca}^{2+}]_i \approx 100\text{ nM}$), $\mathbf{\text{Ca}^{2+}}$ rapidly rushes into the presynaptic terminal.
  • Calcium ions bind to the C2 domains of synaptotagmin-1 (the calcium sensor), triggering the complete zippering of the SNARE complex (syntaxin-1, SNAP-25, and synaptobrevin), which catalyzes the rapid exocytotic fusion of acetylcholine-containing synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic active zone membrane.

question: Resting membrane potential of a neuron range between
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Resting Membrane Potential of Mammalian Neurons:
  • The resting membrane potential ($V_m$) of excitable neuronal membranes is established primarily by:
    1. High intracellular concentration of potassium ($[\text{K}^+]_i \approx 140\text{ mM}$) versus low extracellular potassium ($[\text{K}^+]_o \approx 4\text{ mM}$).
    2. High resting permeability of the membrane to $\text{K}^+$ through constitutively active two-pore domain potassium leak channels ($K_{2P}$).
    3. The electrogenic $\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+$-ATPase pump (pumps $3\,\text{Na}^+$ out for every $2\,\text{K}^+$ in).
  • Because the membrane at rest is predominantly permeable to $\text{K}^+$, the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation yields a resting potential close to the Nernst equilibrium potential for $\text{K}^+$, typically ranging between $-60\text{ mV}$ and $-70\text{ mV}$.

question: The pathological hallmark of Huntington’s disease is
options: The degeneration of the substantia nigra
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Neuropathology of Huntington's Disease:
  • Huntington's Disease (HD): An autosomal dominant, progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat ($>36$ repeats) in the HTT gene, producing a toxic polyglutamine tract in the huntingtin protein.
  • Striatal Degeneration: The hallmark pathological lesion is the profound, selective atrophy and death of GABAergic medium spiny projection neurons in the corpus striatum (specifically the caudate nucleus and putamen) of the basal ganglia.
  • Loss of inhibitory striatal output disinhibits the thalamus, causing the uncontrolled, jerky choreiform movements characteristic of the disease.

question: The patterning of the nervous system along the anterior-posterior axis in embryo is controlled by
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Anterior-Posterior Patterning by Hox (Homeobox) Genes:
  • During embryonic development, the regional specification of the central nervous system along the anterior-posterior (rostral-caudal) axis is orchestrated by the conserved family of Hox genes (Homeobox genes).
  • Hox genes exhibit the remarkable property of spatial and temporal colinearity: their $3'\to5'$ physical order along the chromosome corresponds directly to their spatial expression along the body axis (from anterior hindbrain rhombomeres to posterior spinal cord) and their temporal onset of activation during embryogenesis.

question: Approximately, 50% of total world plant species are present in…
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Global Biodiversity Distribution in Tropical Rainforests:
  • Although tropical rainforest biomes (such as the Amazon Basin, Congo Basin, and Indo-Malayan forests) cover only approximately $6\text{--}7\%$ of the Earth's total land surface area, they are the most biodiverse terrestrial ecosystems on the planet.
  • Due to high year-round solar irradiance, abundant precipitation, warm temperatures, and evolutionary age without recent glaciation disruptions, tropical rainforests are estimated to harbor approximately 50% of all global plant and animal species.

question: The process of mineralization of environmental pollutants by wild microbes is referred as …
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Bioremediation by Microorganisms:
  • Bioremediation: The application of biological mechanisms (using naturally occurring or genetically engineered microorganisms, fungi, or plants) to break down, neutralize, and transform hazardous environmental contaminants and synthetic pollutants into non-toxic, innocuous mineralized end-products (such as $\text{CO}_2, \text{H}_2\text{O}$, and biomass).
  • When conducted by indigenous wild microbial consortia without adding external engineered strains, it is known as intrinsic bioremediation or natural attenuation.

question: Which one of the following is readily available source of nitrogen to plant?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Readily Bioavailable Nitrogen for Plant Roots:
  • Plants absorb inorganic nitrogen from the soil primarily in two ionic forms: ammonium ($\text{NH}_4^+$) and nitrate ($\text{NO}_3^-$).
  • While ammonium ions are positively charged and bind tightly to negatively charged soil clay particles, nitrate ions ($\text{NO}_3^-$) carry a negative charge and remain freely dissolved in the soil aqueous solution.
  • Consequently, nitrate fertilizers are immediately and readily available for rapid uptake by high-affinity nitrate transporters in root epidermal cells.

question: Root nodules are pink due to ….
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Biochemical Basis of Pink Color in Nitrogen-Fixing Root Nodules:
  • Active, functional nitrogen-fixing root nodules of leguminous plants (such as soybean, clover, alfalfa) display a distinct pink-to-red internal pigmentation.
  • Leghemoglobin: A specialized monomeric oxygen-binding hemeprotein synthesized through a true symbiotic partnership: the plant host synthesizes the apoprotein (globin), while the bacteroid (Rhizobium or Bradyrhizobium) synthesizes the iron-porphyrin heme moiety.
  • Oxygen Paradox: The nitrogenase enzyme complex is irreversibly destroyed by oxygen, yet the bacteroids require high rates of oxygen for oxidative ATP production. Leghemoglobin binds oxygen with high affinity, buffering and keeping free oxygen concentration extremely low ($sim 10\text{ nM}$) while maintaining high oxygen flux to the bacterial electron transport chain.

question: Which of the following is a GM phytoremediator plant?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genetically Modified Poplar (Populus) for Phytoremediation:
  • Phytoremediation: The use of green plants to extract, sequester, or detoxify environmental contaminants from polluted soil and groundwater.
  • Genetically Engineered Populus (Poplar): Poplars have extensive, deep root systems and very high transpiration rates. Researchers engineered transgenic poplar trees overexpressing mammalian cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1).
  • These GM poplars exhibit up to 100-fold enhanced capacity to absorb, metabolize, and degrade recalcitrant carcinogenic industrial pollutants, such as trichloroethylene (TCE), carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, and benzene.

question: Which one of the following terms represents the recycling of settled decomposer bacteria in sewage treatment plant?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Activated Sludge Process and Biomass Recycling:
  • Activated Sludge Process (ASP): The most widely utilized secondary biological wastewater treatment technology for domestic and industrial sewage.
  • Wastewater is aerated in an aeration basin where suspended flocs of aerobic microorganisms (bacteria, protozoa, rotifers) metabolize and oxidize dissolved organic matter.
  • The effluent enters a secondary settling tank (clarifier), where biological flocs settle by gravity. To maintain high microbial concentrations and continuous biodegradation in the aeration tank, a significant portion of this settled biological floc is continuously pumped back as Return Activated Sludge (RAS).

question: The relationship between species A and species B is described as commensalism. This means that…..
options: one species benefits and the other species suffers
one species benefits and the other species is unaffected
correct_answer: one species benefits and the other species is unaffected
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Ecological Symbiosis: Commensalism:
  • Commensalism ($+/0$): A positive interspecific ecological interaction where one species benefits while the other species is neither helped nor harmed (unaffected).
  • Examples: Epiphytic orchids growing on tree branches for support without taking nutrients from the tree; remora fish attaching to sharks for free transportation and scraps without harming the shark.
  • (Mutualism is $+/+$; Parasitism/Predation is $+/-$; Amensalism is $-/0$).

question: Which one of the following is the best indicator of SO 2 pollution?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Lichens as Bioindicators of Sulfur Dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$) Pollution:
  • Lichens: Obligate mutualistic symbiotic associations between a fungus (mycobiont) and a photosynthetic alga or cyanobacterium (photobiont).
  • Sensitivity to $\text{SO}_2$: Lichens absorb water, minerals, and gases directly over their entire surface without a protective cuticular waxy layer or roots.
  • Sulfur dioxide gas dissolved in moisture forms toxic sulfurous and bisulfite ions ($HSO_3^-$), which bleach chlorophyll, inhibit photosynthesis, and destroy the algal partner. Consequently, lichens are extraordinarily sensitive to air pollution and serve as classic biological indicators of $\text{SO}_2$ pollution, forming "lichen deserts" downwind of industrial smelters and coal-fired plants.

question: Which one of the following groups of enzymes is primarily involved in microbial bioremediation?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Enzyme Classes in Xenobiotic Biodegradation:
  • The initial catabolic breakdown of persistent environmental pollutants (such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, pesticides, alkanes, and polychlorinated biphenyls) requires activation of recalcitrant chemical bonds.
  • Microorganisms achieve this predominantly through oxygenases (monooxygenases, dioxygenases), peroxidases, and dehydrogenases, which belong to the enzyme class Oxidoreductases (EC 1). These enzymes introduce molecular oxygen or extract electrons to cleave aromatic rings and functionalize hydrocarbon chains for central metabolism.

question: Why catalase is induced in microbes during exposure to the pollutants?
options: Because it involve in biotransformation of that pollutant.
Because of oxidative stress produced due to exposure of pollutant.
Pollutants are general inducers of catalase
Because catalase in involved in the metabolism of metabolite generated from pollutants.
correct_answer: Because of oxidative stress produced due to exposure of pollutant.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Microbial Catalase Induction under Pollutant Exposure:
  • Exposure to environmental pollutants (heavy metals, crude oil, chlorinated pesticides) disrupts normal cellular electron transport and redox homeostasis in microorganisms, triggering the overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS), including superoxide ($O_2^{\bullet-}$) and hydrogen peroxide ($H_2O_2$).
  • To protect essential cellular macromolecules (DNA, membranes, proteins) from lethal oxidative damage, microbial cells activate antioxidant defense operons (such as the OxyR and SoxRS regulons), rapidly inducing catalase to decompose toxic hydrogen peroxide into water and molecular oxygen ($2H_2O_2 \to 2H_2O + O_2$). Thus, catalase is induced in response to pollutant-induced oxidative stress.

question: The solute concentration of the body fluids of some marine organisms are maintained the same as that of the external medium in which the organism lives. Such organisms are referred to as
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Osmoregulation in Marine Invertebrates:
